title: 'One in 50,000': Rare twins born in remote PNG die before help arrives
text:
Medical teams rushing to help a rare pair of conjoined twin girls in remote Papua New Guinea are calling for better referral pathways after the newborns died from heart complications yesterday.

A private airline, doctors and emergency nurses were poised to medically evacuate the sisters from Nonga Base Hospital on the island of New Britain when their condition suddenly deteriorated.

The girls, who had not been named, were joined at the upper abdomen and appeared to be breathing quickly.

Loading...

Janet Sios, who owns a private hospital in Port Moresby that had agreed to treat the twins for free, said their death was a sad outcome.

"We were hoping to help save them both. Our two angels," she wrote in a message to the team involved.

Jurgen Ruh, a pilot who helped transfer another set of conjoined twins born in PNG last year, said assistance should have come earlier.

His non-governmental organisation, Mountain Area Medical Airlift (MAMA) Foundation, found out about the sisters 10 days after they were born.

MAMA quickly mobilised a team of doctors and nurses, with support from a private airline and hospital, and began talks about sending the girls to Australia.

"The ball was rolling and the ball should have been rolling 10 days earlier," Mr Ruh said.

"We can't say they would have certainly made it if they went overseas but certainly they would have had a better chance."

Mr Ruh said doctors treating the conjoined twins at Nonga did their best with extremely limited resources, but failures lay in the country's broader public health system.

"An established referral pathway and early referral would have at least given them a chance to see if they could have survived," he told the ABC.

Chance of conjoined twins is one in 50,000

Last year, Mr Ruh was closely involved in a drawn-out fight to obtain overseas treatment for conjoined twin brothers Tom and Sawong, who were also born in remote PNG.

The boys were eventually transferred to Sydney, where they underwent highly complex surgery that saved Sawong's life.

Cecelia O'Brien, a maternal fetal medicine specialist at James Cook University in Townsville, said it was extremely rare to have two cases of conjoined twins born in such close proximity.

"Conjoined twins are the rarest type of complex twin pregnancies and, in the literature, they occur one in every 50,000 deliveries," she said.

"I mean it doesn't get much rarer than that."

Doctors reveal mission to help conjoined twins A team of doctors involved in the separation of conjoined Papua New Guinean twins Sawong and Tom have spoken for the first time about the rare and complex case.

Dr O'Brien said it was even more unlikely that conjoined twins survived longer than two days after birth.

Without sophisticated imaging and tests, she said it was difficult to say whether faster intervention would have made a difference for the girls.

"It depends on where they were connected as to whether or not they've got a higher or a lower chance of survival," she said.

"If they're just sharing limbs or superficial abdominal wall structures, that's all definitely something that can be divided.

"Babies that share brain, head and neck structures and cardiothoracic structures along with internal abdominal organs, they are the ones that can be very challenging and unpredictable."

She said early diagnosis and access to services like ultrasounds, which are unavailable to many women in PNG, also reduced the risks for mothers.

"The earlier the diagnosis means that there would be a referral system to a maternal fetal medicine specialist," she said.

"Then obviously that family are in the right area, in case they do rupture their membranes early or do have bleeding or end up going into preterm labour."

She hoped solutions being implemented in remote Australia, such as the distribution of portable ultrasound machines, could be transferred to PNG.

title: Emotional return to country with outback station set to become national park
text:
It was an emotional moment for Mike Gilby when his feet sunk into the dirt of his ancestral country for the first time.

For the previous 150 years, the land had been a privately owned station, but now the vast property is among those bought by the New South Wales government to turn into national park.

It means traditional owners such as Mr Gilby, a Malyangapa, Barkandji and Wangkumara man, have been able to set foot on it for the first time.

Growing up in north-west NSW, the lands of his people were his childhood playground, but the private property was off limits.

Setting foot on the former station for the first time felt like reconnecting with family for Mike Gilby. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

"That wasn't as a result of we didn't want to visit. It was a pastoral lease, it was private property and respecting that, you let the pastoralists run it as a business," he said.

"As an adult, coming back here in my late 50s, all those memories are still there, and they're just embedded as part of me."

Mr Gilby was one of more than a dozen traditional owners who recently gathered at the former station, some of them visiting for the first time.

The group was tasked with helping to plan the future of the new national park.

"It just brings back memories as a young black kid growing up out here with all our families, and it wasn't just Aboriginal families, it was everyone. We were a part of the community and we still are today," he said.

Community at forefront of park decisions

The Avenel Mount Westwood reserve encompasses four former pastoral stations with a combined area of 121,000 hectares.

Avenel Mount Westwood Co-management Committee members meet with national parks staff. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

The stations were purchased by the NSW government in 2021 and the park is set to be one of the largest in the state.

The reserve is on the lands of the Malyangapa and Wilyakali people, and representatives from each group make up the Avenel Mt Westwood Aboriginal Co-management Committee, which helps to guide decisions on how the park will be managed.

Mr Gilby said community engagement was at the forefront of their decision-making.

"It's a pastoral area that we operate within, and we need to be considerate of our neighbours who are still operating pastoral properties next door to us," he said.

"But it's also about reconnecting our family, our young people, and putting people back in the landscape, I suppose, under the guise of now working alongside [the National Parks and Wildlife Service].

Committee members are given a tour of the work done so far in the reserve, including the restoration of the old Teilta store. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

" It's setting in place the parameters that the next generations can pick up and take forward. Everything we do at the table today, the beneficiaries are our young people in all of this. "

The NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) estate features a diverse range of ecosystems, including sand plains and sandhills, stony desert, shrubland, rocky hills and flood plain watercourses.

It is also home to 38 different species of threatened flora and fauna.

Aboriginal artefacts have been found across the property, including grinding plates and stones, digging sticks and more, which Mr Gilby said would be preserved and managed with guidance from the committee.

"Now, under [the ownership of NPWS], we're able to look at the landscape through a conservation lens and a cultural lens," he said.

Red sand and big dreams

Looking after the reserve is experienced station manager Makhalia Girdler, who will also live there.

The senior field officer has spent the past 12 years managing the property next door with her husband.

Makhalia Girdler manages and lives on the Avenel Mount Westwood reserve. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

"Running a national park is very similar to managing property, sheep and cattle. There's not much difference in it," she said.

"We're still conserving land, watching the grasses, making sure there's minimal impact."

Managing the reserve means spending most days weeding, maintaining and building station infrastructure and controlling invasive species.

"We're trying to keep the [pig] numbers down. I've been successful with that at the moment; I'm getting hundreds in one night," Ms Girdler said.

The manager, who grew up on a station just down the road, said she could not imagine living anywhere else.

"It's still the isolation, the red sand, that's in my blood. It's my community, my local neighbours. I've known them all my life."

Jaymie Norris and Makhalia Girdler survey a potential lookout site. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

As for the future of the reserve, she has ambitious plans.

"I'd like it to be an education area where we can get the university students back out and study geology or eco-science," she said.

For Mr Gilby, he is excited at the reserve's potential for educating younger generations.

"We want to take the opportunity to actually immerse our next generations back into these landscapes," he said.

"It's about how we leverage off those opportunities to create, be it employment, culture camps, education.

"So it's not just maintaining the biodiversity in the landscape but also [asking], how do we put people back into the landscape to be a part of the bigger picture?"

title: Sandpapergate coach has 'nothing to hide' after forum announced
text:
Former Australian Test coach Darren Lehmann, who led the side during the Sandpapergate incident in 2018, has said he has "nothing to hide" after a new forum into the saga was announced.

Cricket Australia on Wednesday announced a voluntary forum for players and staff involved in the Test match at Cape Town, where Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball, to discuss their recollection and perspective of the incident.

Warner wants Sandpapergate 'public inquiry' as CA announces safe-space forum Cricket Australia has announced a new forum for players and staff to discuss the infamous Sandpapergate scandal, but whether it will achieve anything has already been questioned.

Bancroft, captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner were suspended for their roles in the ball-tampering, but the saga was thrust back into the spotlight last week following the release of Usman Khawaja's memoir, Sabr.

In the book, Khawaja says he knew the ball-tampering was happening, while former player Chadd Sayers has since claimed he believes everyone knew.

Australia's bowling unit has consistently denied they knew about sandpaper being used on the ball.

Lehmann, who has also denied knowing about the ball-tampering plot, has said he supports Cricket Australia's forum.

Darren Lehmann says he will be happy to be part of Cricket Australia's Sandpapergate forum. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Asked if he would be happy to participate while on the ABC Sport broadcast of Australia's third ODI against England, Lehmann said: "Yeah [I would speak to them], I've got nothing to hide."

"I think this gives everyone who didn't get a chance to speak [a chance now].



"It gives everyone a bit of clarity for the Cricket Australia board to make a decision from there [once people are heard]. I think it's a good thing."

The reaction to Khawaja's chapter about Sandpapergate has led to a turbulent fortnight for Australian cricket.

In the book, Khawaja said the whole team should have taken responsibility for the incident and the brunt of punishment should not have been put on Bancroft, Smith and Warner.

Khawaja said he knew the ball-tampering was happening, and even told Bancroft to be careful.

Since the book's release, there has been a frenzy over who knew what and whether the entire team knew of the ball-tampering.

Warner said the claims detailed in Khawaja's book are "100 per cent accurate", and has accused Cricket Australia's 2018 investigation as "botched".

Former Test player Chadd Sayers, who was in the 2018 touring squad, says 'everyone knew' about the use of sandpaper.

Loading...

Current Test captain Pat Cummins held a 70-minute press conference in the wake of the book release, repeating the bowlers' stance that they knew nothing of the ball-tampering, and said his friend had been "casual" with people's lives and reputations.

Lehmann, who will co-host the ABC's cricket podcast this season, said the announcement of a forum by Cricket Australia let him "see some light at the end of the tunnel".

"I haven't been great [for me since the topic re-emerged]," he said.

"People close to me know that. It happened in 2018, it's a long time ago.

"[I] went through health troubles then, and a triple bypass; mentally I wasn't great either.

"The last couple of weeks have been tough, but that's for everyone involved."

title: Thieves steal 1948 Caulfield Cup from Caulfield Racecourse
text:
Thieves have smashed their way into Caulfield Racecourse and stolen the 1948 Caulfield Cup.

That theft is believed to be one in a string of break-ins at the track during Melbourne's Spring Racing carnival.

Victoria Police confirmed this afternoon that an alleged offender or offenders entered the Caulfield premises on four occasions between November 4 and 11.

Red Fury won the 1948 Caulfield Cup. (Supplied)

"Alcohol and trophies, including the Caulfield Cup, were allegedly stolen during the course of offending," the police spokeswoman said.

"A 39-year-old was arrested at a residence on Orrong Road in Elsternwick on 16 November.

"He was charged with attempted burglary and possess drug of dependence (methylamphetamine)."

The police spokeswoman said the Elsternwick man was charged and bailed to attend Moorabbin Magistrates Court on March 1 next year.

A broken display at Flemington Racecourse where three Melbourne Cups won by Makybe Diva were stolen on November 16. (ABC News)

It comes after another brazen heist at Flemington this week, where thieves disguised as construction workers stole three Melbourne Cups won consecutively by legendary mare Makybe Diva in 2003, 2004 and 2005.

"Detectives are investigating if (the Caulfield Cup) incident is linked to the theft of the three Melbourne Cup trophies on 16 November," the police spokeswoman said.

A Melbourne Racing Club spokesman said the cup was stolen along with some bottles of wine and some other "low-value" items.

"The club has been requested by Victoria Police not to speak to the media during the investigation," a MRC spokesman said.

"As this is an active police investigation, the Club can make no further comment at this stage."

It is understood the 1948 Caulfield Cup, won by then five-year-old Australian thoroughbred Red Fury, had been kept in a secure area of the racecourse off-limits to the public.

The cup, worth $55,000, was sold in March and was on loan to the MRC during this year's racing festivities.

Victoria Police has been contacted for comment.

The 2026 theft is not the first time the cup has been stolen.

A painting of Red Fury with jockey William Briscoe with the Caulfield Racecourse grandstand in the background. (Supplied: Leski Auctions)

Three men were committed for trial over the theft of the same 1948 cup, less than two years after Red Fury's racetrack success.

In 1950, The Argus newspaper reported that the cup was stolen from the now-defunct Ress-Astoria Hotel in central Melbourne when it had a value of 200 pounds (about $15,500 in 2026, adjusted for inflation).

One of the men accused of the theft was later acquitted.

title: 'Why are they selling pies?' What surprised O'Connell about AFL footy
text:
When Irish AFLW import Siofra O'Connell arrived in Australia, she wasn't entirely sure what to expect.

She had watched AFL games on TV, time zone permitting, and braced herself for the transition from limited-contact Gaelic football to the heavy contact of Australian Rules.

"I was like, 'This is chaos,'" O'Connell told ABC Sport, who signed for Carlton in December 2024. "It's been a learning curve."

AFLW club culture AFL Players Association CEO James Gallagher says the gap between AFLW clubs getting workplace culture right is widening and the results can be seen on the field.

But then all the quirks and traditions came along with the more than 130-year-old sport.

"I was like, 'Why are they selling pies at a game?' O'Connell laughed. "That was very eye-opening … The chicken and chips is a big one.

"And even the fact that there's alcohol on the ground. You're only allowed it outside the stadium (in Ireland). You can't bring it to your seat.

"So when I went to my first AFL game, and people were a bit tipsy beside me, I didn't know what was going on."

Siofra O'Connell was surprised by the food choices at AFL games. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Media)

Just how much Melbourne is "an AFL city" also took O'Connell by surprise.

"You start getting used to that as well, in a way, because it's on the TV every night of the week almost, and from March to November," she said.

And playing at a big Victorian club like Carlton inevitably puts you in the headlines.

"I work one day a week in the club shop … and that opened my eyes to the supporters and the fan base, and how big the club is," she said.

"You can appreciate it a lot more when it's post-game, and you're engaging with the fans … I'm so not used to all the numbers and spectators. So, it's just amazing to hear a crowd."

Carlton beat Hawthorn in the semifinal to send them to a preliminary final match-up with Melbourne. (Getty: Jonathan DiMaggio)

There was a crowd of over 5,000 for the Blues' qualifying final against North Melbourne, and then about 4,000 for the semifinal against Hawthorn.

"You see the number on the board, and I never would have dreamt that there'd be 5,000 at a game before. (In Ireland), We might go to a game, and we have great support at home, but it's just not as big.

"And the platform isn't as vocal as it is (in Australia)."

Darcy Vescio sealed the semifinal victory for the Blues in their 100th game. (Getty: Jonathan DiMaggio)

That crowd made itself known for the Blues' win over the Hawks in inaugural player and fan-favourite Darcy Vescio's 100th game.

The two-time All Australian sealed the victory with their second goal of the night, prompting the stands to fill with signs celebrating the beloved player.

In the lead-up to the game, Carlton organised speeches honouring Vescio and had special shirts made to mark the occasion.

"Being able to celebrate Darcy today, and seeing that players are getting to 100 games, I just didn't realise how big an achievement it was coming in last season," O'Connell said.

"Because we don't celebrate these kinds of things at home. To see that it's so special, and it's for that person for the week … You're just so excited to go out and play with them, and it lifts you. It lifts your spirits."

title: Minister says scale of WA council woes 'beyond deeply disappointing'
text:
More than two-thirds of local governments in Western Australia have been sanctioned by the local government inspector this year, it has been revealed, over issues ranging from governance challenges to serious misconduct.

WA Local Government Minister Hannah Beazley said "the absolute majority" of the sector had been dysfunctional throughout 2026.

"Over 90 local governments have had action taken against them by the inspector this year, in its very first year of operation, and that is beyond deeply disappointing," she told 102.5 ABC Perth.

A report obtained by the ABC revealed a monitor appointed to oversee the Shire of Serpentine Jarrahdale witnessed conduct that could be contributing to psychosocial safety risks.

Council report details dysfunction A report produced by an independent monitor assigned to work with the Shire of Serpentine Jarrahdale has revealed concerns about councillor behaviour and psychosocial safety.

The monitor estimated that dealing with council member behaviour complaints cost the shire more than $200,000 last financial year.

Multiple councils have had monitors appointed to oversee them this year, including the City of South Perth, City of Perth, Town of Port Hedland and City of Nedlands.

In May, Ms Beazley said it was not sustainable for the state to have 139 local governments, declaring amalgamations back on the table.

The minister today said she was particularly concerned about psychosocial health hazards at the Shire of Serpentine Jarrahdale, which had been referred to WorkSafe.

The idea of council mergers has been floated again amid a string of sackings and dysfunction. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

"Psychosocial health hazards have absolutely no place in local government," she said.

Inspector continuing action

Ms Beazley said the mental health and wellbeing of people working in local government should never be treated as a secondary consideration.

Monitors have been appointed by WA's local government inspector to oversee multiple councils this year. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"The local government inspector has had strong oversight on the issues at the Shire of Serpentine Jarrahdale and to ensure the safety of the workplace — that appropriate action has and will continue to be undertaken," she said.

One of the shire's councillors, Kim Glisenti, this week expressed doubt a 16-point action plan set out by the report would help, calling for stronger action.

Kim Glisenti during his swearing-in as a Serpentine Jarrahdale shire councillor in October last year. (Facebook: Shire of Serpentine-Jarrahdale)

Ms Beazley said she was "astounded" by some of Councillor Glisenti's comments.

"There's an expectation that there's someone stepping in all the time, rather than actually taking personal responsibility [after] someone has stepped in [and] told you what you need to do … now you're saying 'don't do that, step in more'," she said.

Ms Beazley conceded while there were a lot of people in local government "doing the right thing", she had limited capacity to call out their good work and outcomes.

"Unfortunately, I'm not able to concentrate in that space because I have to concentrate on the absolute majority of local governments who have had actions taken against them," she said.

title: Mixed feelings over safer, slower Targa Tasmania rally
text:
Competitors at the Targa Tasmania tarmac rally have expressed mixed reactions to safety measures introduced in the wake of numerous deaths, with one veteran driver saying the changes make the race less competitive.

The annual five-day race from Launceston to Hobart, which began today, stretches across nearly 1,600 kilometres of closed public roads.

Organisers say 40 cars are competing in this year's race and 100 cars in the non-competitive touring event.

Red car at Targa Tasmania start line at the Launceston Silverdome on November 18, 2026. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

Last year, the Targa introduced a series of additional safety restrictions following a coronial inquest into the deaths of four competitors in the 2021 and 2022 races, and this year more have been introduced.

The changes included maximum speed limits for cars in both the race and the tour, changes to the racecourse, and extra rollover protection technology.

While some say the restrictions have undermined the competitive aspect of the race, others say they are necessary to ensure safety.

Each car is equipped with a GPS to monitor its speed. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

Deaths prompt change

First held in 1992, Targa Tasmania has long been a popular event attracting local and interstate drivers to the state, which organisers have said injects around $8 million into the local economy.

But over the years it has changed.

The deaths of three competitors in the 2021 event, followed by the death of another competitor in the 2022 event prompted its cancellation for three years.

Last year, the tarmac rally returned after its hiatus, bringing with it a series of new safety regulations.

The racecourse for this year's Targa Tasmania. (Targa Tasmania)

Stuart Benson, who manages and oversees the course, said the event had received "really strong" positive feedback since introducing the additional safety requirements last year, which have been continued and enhanced this year.

Under the changes introduced last year, each vehicle is given a maximum speed limit based on the category it is racing in, and is fitted with a GPS tracker to monitor the speed.

"If somebody exceeds the acceptable limits that apply to both the touring and competition categories, we become aware of that in real time and penalties can be applied, as well as policing and compliance of that," Mr Benson said.

" [This] could range from time penalties to exclusion from the event depending on the level of the offence. "

Stuart Benson says the new safety measures have been received positively. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

The race course has also been reconfigured since last year, with 10 of the 41 stages of the race new and 12 of them revised.

Changes to the size requirements of the roll cages — the metal structures inside the car which protect the driver if the car rolls over — have also been implemented.

New roll cage requirements are in place to help protect drivers if they crash and roll. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

Safety regulations hamper competition, one driver says

Perth driver Peter Rullo first raced in Targa in 2011, and has competed ever since, last year placing second.

He understands why the safety measures were brought in, but said they caused "hiccups" last year, which he hopes have since been smoothed out.

"There was less competition, so a lot of the stages were very easy to achieve the base time which meant there wasn't competition between the cars," he said.

Peter Rullo understands why changes have been implemented, but believe some reduce competition. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

Mr Rullo said the field of competitors at the rally had become "quite small".

"When I first started coming to Targa, this whole venue would have been full of cars, and there would have been cars outside," he said.

He said certain "fast parts" of stages had been removed, such as one through Cethana in the state's north-west.

"There's a fast long straight section, so that section we're restricted to 80 kilometres per hour now, where previously we could get close to 200 kilometres an hour," Mr Rullo said.

Other drivers praise changes

Launceston driver Crichton Lewis does not agree the safety precautions have impacted competition.

"Roll cage changes don't really affect the race at all. Speed limiting, good idea," he said.

Targa Tasmania has both competitive and non-competitive categories. (Instagram: Targa Tasmania)

Like Mr Rullo, Glenn Ridge is also a long-time participant, having competed in every Targa since 1993 except last year's.

He said the sport's had a "tumultuous" last couple of years, which he believes had "taken its toll".

"[Targa isn't] quite like it was with the numbers we had 10 years ago where there were 300 cars going around. But I think it will build up," he said.

Former television personality Glenn Ridge says the number of competitors has reduced in recent years. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

Mr Ridge said after the deaths, it was clear "things needed to change" and he said most people were understanding.

"There are a lot of people who are pushing the barriers, I guess."

" There's a lot of talk out there and everyone's trying to scaremonger things … but at the end of the day, everyone in this building here knows the reasons they're put into play. "

The race will conclude on November 22.

title: Brisbane's Olympic stadium ahead of schedule but questions on costs swirl
text:
Early works at Brisbane's Victoria Park precinct are ahead of schedule, with construction on the stadium expected to begin mid-2027.

But the price tag for the substantial earthworks, ahead of the city hosting the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games, remains hidden.

It has also been revealed taxpayers will be slugged with the cost of the Gabba demolition.

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said 200,000 cubic metres of soil and rock had already been excavated.

Early works are underway on Brisbane Stadium at Victoria Park ahead of the Olympic and Paralympic Games. (Supplied: COX Architecture and Hassell)

"That is the equivalent of 80 Olympic swimming pools of dirt moved in 100 days in preparation for the Brisbane Stadium," he said.

"And in the middle, you will see two AFL footballs, and those two AFL footballs are the centre bounce for the Brisbane Lions' first game when the Brisbane Stadium opens."

An artist's impression of the new Brisbane Stadium at Victoria Park. (Supplied: Queensland Government)

Mr Bleijie was forced to defend the state government forking out $600 million in public funds to developers for the new Brisbane arena at Woolloongabba.

The $1.4 billion arena will be delivered in partnership with the private sector by 2031.

Successful Brisbane Arena tenderer revealed Gather Brisbane has been chosen to build the $1.4 billion Brisbane Arena at Woolloongabba, and to develop the former Gabba site after the stadium is torn down following the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

The deputy premier was asked why taxpayers needed to be charged at all.

"Because when you partner with the private sector to deliver things, that's how you can deliver. Otherwise, it will not happen," Mr Bleijie said.

"The state does not give a cent to the consortia until it operates and the stadium is finished, built, and open.

"Then that is offset by the sale of the land, and it may be even a bit more. The value of the land may even be more than 600."

Mr Bleijie could not put an exact figure on what the financial return would be to taxpayers.

A render of Brisbane's Victoria Park stadium set up to host a concert. (Supplied: Queensland government)

Question swirl over the Gabba

An independent report into Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic venue options noted significant upgrades would be needed to the Gabba to make it Games-ready.

While the sports program is not expected to be locked in until next year, the government has flagged it could host cricket if included.

The report found the Gabba was not compliant with disability requirements, and needed a range of work, including to its roofing and lighting.

But Mr Bleijie assured the government would not be throwing money at upgrading the near end-of-life stadium.

"It'll be very minimal because we're going to knock it down after the 2032 Games," he said.

Taxpayers are set to have to pay for the demolition of the Gabba. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Mr Bleijie also revealed taxpayers will need to fund the cost of its demolition.

While there has been no recent standalone cost to demolish the stadium, a full rebuild was estimated to be almost $3 billion.

"The state will be responsible. It's a state asset, so of course we're responsible," Mr Bleijie said.

Speaking alongside Mr Bleijie, Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority (GIICA) chair Stephen Conry, said the design of the National Aquatic Centre was being finalised.

A render of the proposed National Aquatic Centre released by the Queensland government in July. (Supplied: Queensland government)

The venue will replace Brisbane's Centenary Pool, with a Games capacity currently of 25,000 seats.

"It might be more or less than that," Mr Conry said.

"We're in that final stage of the design, and when you're dealing with public money, you want to get the design right."

He said a projection validation report on Rockhampton's Fitzroy River hosting rowing and canoeing at the Games would be completed in the "first half of next year".

title: Woolworths shoppers call for answers over gift card draining issue
text:
Frustrated customers who have lost hundreds of dollars from drained Woolworths gift cards are calling on the supermarket giant to explain what happened and warn others who may be affected.

Woolworths apologised to affected customers on Monday, saying it recognised the concern the issue had caused and was investigating reports as a priority.

But Woolworths has declined to comment on what caused the issue or disclose how many shoppers lost money, despite earlier acknowledging a problem affecting "a number of customer e-gift cards".

Woolworths did not say whether the issue was contained. (ABC News)

The ABC has heard from more customers across Australia who say their Everyday WISH gift cards were drained without their knowledge over the past week, reporting losses of up to $500.

All had purchased their cards digitally through the Everyday Rewards website or app during a promotional period offering 4 per cent off gift cards.

Transaction histories seen by the ABC show payments to stores customers say they did not visit. In other cases, transactions are listed against an online store or a generic descriptor without identifying a store or location.

Experts say there are several possible explanations for the losses, including an "enumeration attack" or software vulnerability, but they caution there is not enough information so far to determine what happened.

'You should be alerting us'

Paul Hobbs, from Brisbane, said he was frustrated Woolworths had not been more proactive in communicating about the issue.

"If you're serious about customers and you're concerned about some transactions that have happened, whether you can explain it or not, you should be reaching out to customers and alerting us," Mr Hobbs said.

Mr Hobbs, who started using gift cards to pay for his groceries because it was more economical, discovered on Monday that his card had been drained without his knowledge.

His transaction history showed a payment of $210.16 described as "Woolworths Group Limited Services", but did not specify a store or location.

Paul Hobbs says the unauthorised transaction was listed against a generic descriptor of "Woolworths Group Limited Services". (Supplied)

"Woolworths should have made me aware of this so that I don't stress about where the funds have gone, rather than rely on me finding out elsewhere," he said.

"They always tell you the customer is important to them, but they're happy for something strange to happen and stay silent."

Mr Hobbs said he had not shared his card details and Woolworths had not warned him about a potential problem.

Concerns over a data breach

Chris Lang, from Hobart, said he wanted to know whether there had been a data breach after he lost his entire gift card balance to purchases he did not recognise.

"Losing up to $500 is no small thing," he said.

" It's pretty unpleasant to be second guessing your passwords and computer security. "

He said he had emailed the gift card support address provided by the company but had so far received only an automated acknowledgement.

"It would be nice for Woolworths to communicate what's going on," he said.

"It's hard to know how to react without some indication of what the issue is."

Woolworths apologises after customers report gift card draining Woolworths has acknowledged an issue affecting a number of customer e-gift cards and is investigating, with replacement cards among the possible next steps for affected customers.

Sydney man Michael Bennett previously told the ABC his e-gift card had disappeared from his digital wallet after a $400 balance was drained.

Mr Bennett said he got in touch with a Woolworths representative who described the problem as an "IT malfunction" and said there had been no security breach.

Woolworths has not publicly confirmed that explanation.

Debbie Kellie, who also lost $500, previously told the ABC she had deactivated her Visa card as a precaution and that the matter had been referred to Queensland police.

All the customers the ABC spoke to insisted they did not share their card details with anyone or accidentally disclose them to a spoof website.

Experts outline possible causes

Woolworths said on Monday its team would work directly with customers to determine appropriate next steps, including issuing replacement e-gift cards.

Customers who notice unrecognised transactions have been advised to contact Gift Card Support or log into the Everyday Gifting website and register their details on its home page.

But when asked by the ABC whether the issue had been contained and whether customers' personal information may have been compromised, Woolworths declined to comment.

Adam Parks, a former Australian representative for the US Department of Homeland Security's investigative unit, said the incident was unlikely to involve physical tampering with gift cards.

He is in the US, where he heads a Homeland Security taskforce dedicated to investigating gift card fraud.

Adam Parks is the head of US taskforce that investigates gift card fraud. (Supplied: Adam Parks)

Mr Parks said he suspected one of two possible scenarios.

The first was an "enumeration attack", where criminals use automated programs or bots to generate large numbers of possible gift card numbers and check them against an online balance checker.

Once a valid card number with an available balance is identified, criminals can potentially use the information to drain the funds.

The second possibility was that customers had entered their gift card details into a fraudulent website designed to look like a legitimate balance-checking service.

"I understand they deny doing so, but most victims say that and don't realise they were scammed," he said.

Mr Parks said organised criminals went to considerable lengths to direct customers to fake websites, including paying for search engine optimisation and using AI to mimic the look and feel of legitimate services.

"It's extremely difficult to tell the difference," he said.

"So I suspect they had their [gift card] numbers stolen when checking their balance."

Micheal Axelsen, an associate professor in information systems at the University of Queensland, said it was difficult to determine what had happened without more information from Woolworths.

"It could be caused by any one of a dozen things," he said.

Dr Axelsen said potential explanations included a software vulnerability, an unpatched server, weaknesses in gift card security controls or fraudulent activity by someone with internal access to the system.

He said automated tools, including those powered by AI, could allow malicious actors to identify and exploit software vulnerabilities much faster than in the past.

Coles investigates cyber attack Coles has told customers to "remain vigilant" as it investigates a cyber incident.

The Australian Signals Directorate's Australian Cyber Security Centre has separately warned organisations about the increasing speed at which software vulnerabilities are being exploited.

In an alert issued the day after the ABC reported on the gift card issue and a separate cybersecurity breach at Coles, the agency said malicious actors were exploiting unpatched vulnerabilities to gain access to systems, steal data and take control of networks.

The alert did not refer to Woolworths or Coles.

The agency generally urged organisations to accelerate security updates, strengthen identity and access controls, and monitor systems for suspicious activity.

So You Are, ridden by Rachel King, on its way to the barriers before competing in the Melbourne Cup at Flemington earlier this month. Kids and adults can be big fish in a small pond at Brisbane Powerhouse this summer. Open Ocean – an interactive gaming experience by Brisbane’s acclaimed Dead Puppet Society involving large robot fish in an immersive reef environment – is the centrepiece of a new summer festival at the Powerhouse titled Summer Playground. The Queensland government has splashed $250,000 on the production – one of five ambitious works given funding to amaze audiences in the lead-up to the Olympics. Open Ocean is an interactive experience by Dead Puppet Society at Brisbane Powerhouse. Dean Hanson “You get given a remote and you control a life-size sailfish on an adventure through a series of different Australian ecosystems,” said David Morton, creative director of Dead Puppet Society.

“Dead Puppets has been creating creatures for almost two decades now, but this is the first time we’ve handed control of our creations over to the audience.” Summer Playground is an eight-week festival of art, play and sport for all ages, with nine free and ticketed events taking place at the Brisbane Powerhouse in January and February 2027. Players chase prey and explore an immersive reef environment. Dean Hanson They include Anthem Anthem Revolution, where players compete against a table tennis robot. Louise Bezzina, artistic director and chief executive of Brisbane Powerhouse. Broken Hill Gold’s demerged Queensland gold assets are set to join the new Manda Resources IPO, in a value-unlocking event for existing shareholders. Notably, Manda has also attracted the backing of multi-billion-dollar gold producer Emerald Resources, which will provide $5.24 million in backing to the planned IPO and emerge as one of the company’s major shareholders. Advance Metals and Sky Metals recently proposed combining five Victorian and New South Wales gold projects into a new ASX-listed explorer targeting a $6 million IPO. That proposed transaction highlights the appeal of consolidating exploration assets into separately funded vehicles rather than leaving them embedded within diversified small-cap companies. In addition to the free share distribution, eligible Broken Hill shareholders will get a priority offer to subscribe for up to $2 million of the Manda IPO for around four million shares, if they wish to follow the Queensland promise. White Dam historically produced 180,000 ounces between 2010 and 2018 and comes with open pits, heap-leach infrastructure and an operational gold extraction plant, giving the company a brownfields springboard rather than a standing-start development. The near-mine grounds span Vertigo and Hannaford alongside the emerging Icebreaker gold-copper discovery, with existing processing infrastructure providing a ready pathway for shallow oxide material.

Ben Carroll’s hopes of leaning on Labor’s economic legacy to hold on to power at the state election have been dealt a blow by figures showing Victoria is the nation’s economic laggard. Figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics released on Wednesday showed the state’s economy grew by 1.7 per cent through 2025-26. Premier Ben Carroll speaking with voters at a pre-poll centre in his electorate. Louis Trerise Every other state and territory posted stronger growth, led by the Northern Territory, which expanded by 3.2 per cent, and Queensland at 3.1 per cent. The nation’s largest state economy, NSW, grew by 2.1 per cent. On a per-capita basis, Victoria was also dragging down the national economic chain with zero growth. The best performers were the NT and Tasmania, which grew by 1.6 per cent. In NSW, it was 0.9 per cent.

Advertisement

Separate data released on Wednesday showed wages grew by 3.3 per cent in Victoria in the 12 months to September. Only the ACT registered slower wage growth. After inflation, Victorian wages fell by 0.2 per cent through the year. Carroll, who attended the pre-polling booth this morning, struggled to talk around a previous Labor voter upset at the business conditions facing him and the state. “Well, I had the opportunity to talk to him,” Carroll told reporters about the interaction. “He has been a previous Labor voter, and I wanted to make it very clear he was fairly supportive of me in the new direction.

“That was why I said I am going to cut land tax, I am a pro-business premier, and they’re the conversations that we get to have every day with voters just like him.” But pressed on whether he had changed the voter’s mind, Carroll admitted failure. “[I] don’t think I convinced him at the end,” he said. “He was very respectful, and it was a good conversation. He knew who I was, knew my background, but that’s democracy.” Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said the state economy was struggling because of the government’s tax policies.

Advertisement

“After 12 years of Labor, Victoria has the weakest economic growth of any state or territory and the weakest wage growth of any state in the country,” she said. “Our population is growing, but economic output per Victorian is going nowhere.” Victoria’s performance last financial year was held back by a sharp fall in mining activity amid a drop in oil and gas production. The strongest part of the economy was financial and insurance services, while there was also a lift in healthcare and social assistance demand. An increase in school and university construction also bolstered the economy. The 1.7 per cent rise last year followed growth of 1.6 per cent in 2024-25 and 1.5 per cent the previous year.

Over the past decade, Victoria’s performance has been one of the strongest in the Commonwealth. Since 2015-16, the economy has grown by almost 27 per cent, eclipsing NSW (21.7 per cent), Western Australia (19.4 per cent), South Australia (25.2 per cent) and the NT (14.8 per cent). The fastest growing part of the country over the past decade has been the ACT, where the economy has expanded by more than 40 per cent. On a per-capita basis, Victoria’s growth of 8.4 per cent has also outperformed jurisdictions including NSW (8.1 per cent), Queensland (7.1 per cent) and the NT (4.8 per cent). I’ve been a racehorse trainer for more than 30 years and never in my life have I seen a deceased horse dumped in a skip bin – until Tuesday. The photos and videos of Melbourne Cup runner So You Are being disposed of at a Lucas Heights dump after dying of colic were shocking and disturbing, and everyone in the racing industry I’ve spoken to in the past 48 hours feels the same way. So You Are, ridden by Rachel King, parades prior to the running of the Lexus Melbourne Cup at Flemington. Racing Photos via Getty Images No animal deserves to be treated that way, and now the spotlight is on industry leaders to see how they respond. We live on a property, and for different reasons, we have had to have horses put down here. We have quite a big property so we bury horses properly when we can, and take comfort in knowing we’re doing the right thing and respecting the horse.

Advertisement

When a horse has to be put down at a veterinary clinic – and that happens quite a lot too – I always thought they would bury them because they charge you, and so you believe they are being disposed of properly. To find out that’s not the case, at least in this instance, is shocking. In all my time in racing, and having grown up around horses, I have never heard of anything like this happening. So You Are was found dumped in a skip bin at Lucas Heights in Sydney. Facebook This kind of incident is also extremely damaging to the racing industry, and it’s not the kind of practice we want to see. We love our horses, and the past 48 hours have been frustrating and sad. There’s got to be a better way. The fact is, disposing of a deceased horse is a problem for any horse owner, not just racehorse owners. But So You Are was a racehorse, and because the racing industry is so big, people will be looking to it.

Advertisement

There is no doubt Racing NSW is on the front foot and looking at what it can do to make sure this doesn’t happen again. The situation here is black and white and something has to change. Knowing what we know now, that it is common practice for horses to end up in landfill, there needs to be reforms to how we dispose of deceased horses. One idea is for the industry to invest in a crematorium, so trainers, owners and jockeys know their racehorses are being treated with dignity in death. That would also mean that deceased horses wouldn’t be taking up space in landfill, and horrific situations like what we’ve seen in the past 48 hours wouldn’t occur.

Advertisement

For most of us in the industry, we are part of racing because we love horses, not just the competition. Related Article Opinion

Racing integrity So You Are’s horrifying final fate in a skip bin with an old couch is beyond unacceptable Neil Breen National sports editor We’ve got about 20 horses in work at the moment, but we are constantly getting horses and retiring horses. Some are become broodmares and some are just nice horses we keep around the farm because we love them. But for the most part, we spend a significant amount of time, money and effort into retraining and re-homing them so they have long lives and good homes. It makes me so happy to see my horses have another life after racing. Reform won’t happen overnight, but from the time a horse is born to the time of its death, everything should be done respectfully, and I think a crematorium would be a good way to make things work.

Working Australians buying homes have endured a year of falling real wages on top of soaring mortgage repayments as signs grow the economy will struggle into 2027. The Australian Bureau of Statistics this morning reported the wage price index rose by a higher-than-expected 1.1 per cent in the September quarter. Real wages have gone backwards for the fourth consecutive quarter. Oscar Colman It was driven by this year’s minimum wage increase of 4.75 per cent and was the largest quarterly increase since the end of 2023. It took annual wage growth to 3.5 per cent. Despite that, inflation through to the September quarter was 3.9 per cent. It meant in real terms, wages went backwards by 0.4 per cent. It was the fourth successive quarterly negative result for real wages.

Advertisement

Apart from the minimum wage increase, a series of state-based pay increases to frontline public servants including nurses, midwives and police officers contributed to the out-sized quarterly result. Related Article Live

National News Live Australia news as it happened: Labor blames high inflation for falling wages; Cook cuts deal to exempt WA gas from national scheme Treasurer Jim Chalmers said nominal wages growth had exceeded 3 per cent for 17 consecutive quarters, the first time they had been that strong for 17 years. “Labor’s support for higher wages is helping almost 2.8 million workers on the national minimum wage, up to 460,000 health, disability and community services workers and the 400,000 strong aged care work force,” he said. Wages for the bottom 20 per cent of earners rose by 4.7 per cent over the past 12 months, largely due to the minimum wage increase, while for the next 20 per cent they grew by 3.9 per cent.

Advertisement

But deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume said once inflation was taken into account, Australians were going backwards. “[The] figures confirm what every Australian already knows: their pay packet buys less now than it did when Labor came to office. Australians aren’t just feeling poorer, they are poorer,” she said. Since mid-2022, soon after the government took office, inflation has climbed by a combined 18.2 per cent. Over that same period, wages have increased by 16.2 per cent. That followed the Morrison government period in office when real wages also went backwards. Over the past 8 years, wages have grown by 25.9 per cent compared to inflation which has risen by 31.5 per cent.

Advertisement

The figures were released as Westpac’s measure of economic activity in coming months fell into negative territory. The bank is now expecting economic growth to slow to 1.4 per cent in 2026 and the drop to just one per cent next year. EY chief economist Cherelle Murphy said while the wage figures would not prompt an immediate response from the Reserve Bank. “The figure is uncomfortably high for the central bank but is unlikely to prompt any immediate reaction given the economy is now slowing in response to the five interest rate hikes delivered between February and November this year,” she said. “The Reserve Bank is tackling the challenge by aggressively trying to bring inflation down. Given the significant rise in the cash rate from 3.6 to 4.85 per cent this year, we expect the central bank will be in wait-and-see mode.” That could be challenged by job figures due out on Thursday. Unemployment has lifted to a five-year high of 4.7 per cent, with forward indicators suggesting the jobs market is slowing.

Advertisement

The single largest increase was for people in the hospitality sector, which is broadly covered by the minimum wage decision. Wages for these workers lifted by 3.4 per cent in the quarter to be 4.1 per cent up over the year. Wages in the education sector are the slowest growing in the country, up 0.8 per cent in the quarter but just 2.6 per cent over the past 12 months. Professional services (2.7 per cent) and those in administration and financial services (both 2.9 per cent) are also a long way behind inflation. Private sector wages rose to 3.4 per cent while public sector wages lifted by 3.9 per cent over the past year. Larvotto Resources has received a massive vote of confidence from its offtake partners, securing a combined US$30 million (A$45M) prepayment for future concentrate supply from its Hillgrove gold-antimony mine in New South Wales. The funding coup comes as the company dispatched its first shipment of gold concentrate to commodities giant Glencore, marking a pivotal step in its transition to a multi-commodity producer. The company says it has received the full US$30 million, with Glencore and Wogen Resources each providing US$15 million. The 12-month prepayment facility is designed to bolster working capital as the Hillgrove processing plant navigates its four-month commissioning phase, which is expected to be finalised by the end of this year. Larvotto Resources has dispatched its first gold concentrate from the Hillgrove mine in New South Wales. The prepayments will be settled through future deliveries of gold and antimony concentrates. This financial backing coincides with a significant operational achievement, with the first shipment of gold concentrate now on its way to Glencore’s warehouse in Brisbane. The delivery follows Larvotto’s maiden antimony concentrate shipment to Wogen in October, establishing a second revenue stream for the company.

Advertisement

Management says it is also advancing metallurgical testwork on the project’s tungsten resource, with about two tonnes of sample material en route to Canada for flowsheet optimisation. It is eyeing potential tungsten production in 2027, which would add a third critical mineral to its product suite. ‘Focus is now on gold concentrate production with tonnes and grade improving steadily.’ Larvotto Resources managing director Ron Heeks The market for both antimony and tungsten is becoming increasingly strategic, with western economies scrambling to secure supply chains outside of China and Russia. Operations controlled by the two nations account for roughly 80 per cent of global antimony supply, a mineral deemed “critical” by Australia, the US and the European Union for its use in defence and energy storage. Similarly, China dominates the tungsten market, producing about 79 per cent of the world’s supply. The strategic importance of non-Chinese sources is set to intensify, with US defence procurement rules restricting tungsten from China and Russia scheduled to take effect in January 2027. With its Hillgrove project forecast to become Australia’s largest antimony producer, Larvotto appears well-placed to capitalise on this shifting geopolitical landscape.

The company is now ramping up its processing plant toward full production, with the first gold doré pour anticipated in late November. Forecast annual production from Hillgrove is pegged at 40,500 ounces of gold and 4,900 tonnes of antimony. Larvotto Resources managing director Ron Heeks said: “Our first gold concentrate delivery to Glencore is another milestone in Hillgrove’s ramp-up. With gold and antimony concentrate now delivered, we are building diversified revenue streams. The Australian-dollar gold price has risen from approximately A$3,100 per ounce when we acquired Hillgrove to A$5,750 today. This provides a supportive backdrop to our forecast annual gold production of 40,500 ounces.” Since commissioning began, Larvotto says the processing plant has performed to plan, with tonnes and grade steadily improving and on track with forecasts. Antimony production was commissioned first and is reportedly running close to optimal levels. Larvotto snapped up Hillgrove from administrators in October 2023 for a bargain $8 million, including a $5 million environmental bond. The project hosts a formidable resource of 1.7 million gold-equivalent ounces at a healthy grade of 7.4 grams per tonne gold equivalent, highlighting the scale of the prize Larvotto secured for a relative song. With an extra US$30 million in the bank from two of the biggest names in the global commodities trade and both its primary products now being shipped, Larvotto is quickly shedding its developer skin. title: Trump's AI push has Albanese's signature, but another country is quickly gaining ground
text:
In brief Donald Trump said he and the leaders of Australia, India and Japan are working together to "advance super intelligence".

Australia is one of several signatories to a US-led initiative aimed at securing the supply chains needed for AI development.

Technology capability and cybersecurity were prominent topics during Tuesday night's Quad meeting in the Philippines, with the leaders of Australia, the United States, Japan and India affirming support for US-led development on artificial intelligence.

In a joint press statement, the leaders said: "We are securing critical supply chains, protecting freedom of navigation and overflight, driving growth through technologies of the future including investments in and deployment of trusted Super Intelligence (SI)*".

That asterisk pointed to a clarification further down.

"*In Australia, India, and Japan, 'Super Intelligence' refers to 'artificial intelligence,'" it said.

The phrase has been a regular addition to joint statements since US President Donald Trump's executive order in September to replace the term "artificial intelligence" with "super intelligence" in all official US communications to better reflect "the full promise and opportunity of these technologies".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

AI and the resources needed for its use and development continue to shape international diplomacy, as the US and China compete for technological advancement.

Olivia Shen, the director of the strategic technologies program at the United States Studies Centre, has been to multiple Quad meetings over the years.

"Technology cooperation has always been a really important stream of work under the Quad," she told SBS News.

"So it makes sense that now we're looking at these announcements that expand on that by looking at the things that people are really worried about right now."

Key concerns include the security of undersea cables, the protection of critical mineral supply chains, and cybersecurity, particularly with advances in AI.

It's one of several disconnects developing between the view of artificial intelligence promoted by US leaders and its reception in wider society, as AI infrastructure proves divisive in communities internationally and shapes election results.

Australia signs on to US-led declaration on AI supply chain

This week, Australia, India and Japan were among 10 countries that signed a US-led declaration to strengthen controls on supply chains critical to AI development.

The San Francisco Declaration reinforces collective responsibility to protect sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure from undue influence. A spokesperson for Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the joint statement was about ensuring the technologies and supply chains Australia relied on were secure.

The agreement was part of Trump's broader Pax Silica initiative, an alliance aimed at building a global supply chain for the technology and infrastructure needed for AI among the US and allied countries. It excludes China, which has a dominant lead in producing and refining critical minerals used in AI hardware and other infrastructure.

Launched in December last year, it now has 26 signatories — including Australia, Japan and India, as well as the United Kingdom, South Korea, Singapore, and Israel.

In the Philippines, another Pax Silica signatory, the initiative has sparked protests over a proposal to build a 1,600-hectare industrial hub to support semiconductor manufacturing, the processing of critical minerals, and other AI infrastructure.

(Left to right) Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese met on the sidelines of the 2026 ASEAN summit in Manila. Source: AAP / Lukas Coch

Activists opposed to the project say it will displace members of the Indigenous Aeta community and local farmers and strain water and electricity supplies.

In the capital Manila, thousands of people took part in demonstrations this week criticising Trump's arrival and — among other issues — calling for the Philippines to reject involvement in Pax Silica.

After Tuesday night's meeting, Trump said the Quad countries were working together to "advance super intelligence", which he called "the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the industrial revolution".

"And it's working out amazingly well," he told reporters.

Shen isn't so convinced.

"Things are not going overly well," she said.

"The reality is that US frontier models are still more advanced than Chinese rivals at this point in time, but they're about five to six months ahead of the curve."

Chinese models are gaining popularity, offering more affordable options to consumers and often released as open-weight products, enabling tweaks that let users fine-tune the model.

"The US, in a way, they're quite right that the US AI technologies win on performance and probably on security as well, considering China's past history of building in back doors and surveillance technologies into their hardware and software," Shen said.

"But I think the trend lines show that the economics of what China's offering, is getting a lot of traction."

China has also been leading its own push for collaboration through the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, which has 37 member countries, including Russia and Iran. Its signatories include 15 countries in Asia, 13 in Africa, four in Europe and five in the Americas.

"That's seen as a bit of a rival to the US-led Pax Silica initiative that is all about securing and safeguarding AI supply chains," Shen said.

"What the US is trying to offer is that countries around the world can become great by adopting the American technology stack because they have a lead over China.

"And particularly for countries that are very worried about cybersecurity and security of critical infrastructure, then they probably do want to go with the best models and they may be willing to pay a premium for it."

However, China remains excluded from access to the US' advanced chips.

Trump's government on Monday moved to close a loophole that allowed Chinese companies to train on technology from companies like Nvidia at data centres in other countries.

Some Chinese companies aren't reliant on renting US tech for training AI models so won't be affected by the crackdown but there will likely be an overall dampening on China's capabilities, Kyle Chan, a fellow in the John L Thornton China Center at The Brookings Institution, told the ABC.

He said the competition between China and the US is "very intense... but lopsided" as the US has technological advantages, while China is more focused on integrating powerful AI models into the rest of its economy.

Australia's role in the supply chain

"In terms of the bilateral relationship between Australia and the US, there is a strong sense that the US sees Australia as an important partner on critical minerals and rare earths," Shen said.

This has become more important as China has sought to restrict the access of other Quad nations over the past several years.

Rare earths are needed for electronics, semiconductors, magnets, alloys and advanced materials used in anything from data centres to jet engines.

"Rare earths are just a really important part of the supply chain where you want more diversity and we want more resilience rather than being beholden to a single source that could use that against us," Shen said.

title: State wins carve-out from plan to make gas cheaper, but Labor still facing battle in the Senate
text:
IN BRIEF Labor has proposed an amendment that would allow WA's gas reservation obligation to be permanently set at zero.

Under the proposal, the scheme would remain equal across other states and territories.

The Western Australian gas reservation won't be impacted at all by an east-coast scheme, under further assurances attached to a government bill that has been stalled in the Senate.

The federal government is trying to pass plans for an east coast gas reservation scheme, which would force liquefied natural gas exporters to reserve up to 20 per cent of their annual exports for domestic use.

Western Australia had become a sticking point for the opposition and state leaders over how a national reserve could affect its existing gas reservation scheme, in operation since 2006.

A last-minute amendment was circulated on Wednesday morning, which would allow the federal minister to permanently set Western Australia's gas reservation obligation for the national scheme to zero.

title: Regional house prices fall as cautious investors flee
text:
Escaping the city rat race has never looked better, with regional house prices falling as cautious investors flee.

National regional dwelling values fell 2 per cent in the past three months, almost double the rate of the previous quarter, according to market data released on Wednesday.

Queensland's regions led the decline, falling 2.7 per cent, followed by NSW at 2.1 per cent, Cotality's regional market update showed.

"Regional markets have held up better than the capitals, but they're not immune to the same pressures," the data firm's head of research Gerard Burg said.

The Gold Coast, Tweed, Bundaberg, Maryborough and Gladstone regions, which have all been hot spots for sea changers, led declines in Queensland.

Marked slowdown after years of strong demand

Brad Barth, the principal at Belle property in Bundaberg, said the lower end of the market had taken the biggest hit, with the price of new homes remaining relatively stable.

It had been a marked slowdown after years of frenzied demand and population growth, Barth said.

"Because there was no stock, everything was almost coming up to the same level," he told the Australian Associated Press.

"You'd have a beautiful, neat home getting snapped up in a couple of days and one that was a lot rougher in a different spot.

"Someone who missed out on the neat home ... would then pay a similar price for the other home."

Regional value drops have not been as pronounced as metro markets, which had combined falls of 4.5 per cent.

A 30.6 per cent decline in investor lending was driven in part by curbs to negative gearing and Labor's capital gains tax discount, the Australian Bureau of Statistics said on November 11.

Rising interest rates were already sending property values downwards and investors retreating from the market at a greater rate than owner-occupiers.

A drop in NSW regional values was led by Ballina, in the Northern Rivers, Morisset–Cooranbong and Nelson Bay, in the Hunter, and Wollongong, south of Sydney.

Busselton, on Western Australia's south coast, had the steepest decline among the 50 largest regional centres, at 4.1 per cent.

At the other extreme, the state's mining hub Kalgoorlie-Boulder recorded the strongest quarterly growth at 3.4 per cent.

Regional South Australia and the Northern Territory were the only regional markets to record quarterly growth, up 0.1 per cent and 2.2 per cent, respectively, while Victoria experienced a modest decline of 1.5 per cent.

The report said local employment and economic confidence would determine which regional markets held up.

'A pretty good place to live'

Barth said Bundaberg continued to represent good value.

"Teachers, nurses, doctors might be earning slightly less here, but then everything costs slightly less," he said.

title: There might be a reason your rental has more problems, research suggests
text:
IN BRIEF Housing experts analysed national data to compare the differences in renting through an agent and a landlord.

Renters dealing with agents were more likely to report delayed repairs or unjustified rent increases.

Just a few decades ago in Australia, renting was widely seen as a stepping stone for students and young people on their way to owning a home.

Now, more Australians are renting and making rental properties a place to call home in the long term.

In many states and territories, rental laws have started to catch up, with stronger rights and protections for tenants.

Much of the debate about renting more broadly focuses on the rights of renters or the needs of landlords.

An important group is often overlooked: real estate agents and property managers.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Our new research suggests whether you rent through an agent or directly from a landlord can make a big difference.

We found tenants who were dealing with agents were more than twice as likely to say they experienced common problems.

Who manages your rental issues

Around 80 per cent of privately rented homes in Australia are rented out via agents, rather than directly from a landlord.

Agents often play a major role in renters' lives. This includes deciding who gets a property in the first place, coordinating repairs, and setting and adjusting rents.

Agents are chosen and retained by landlords. But the agent is the main, often only, person that renters can contact about their homes.

Other renters deal directly with their landlord. And the same tenancy laws apply to both arrangements. But agents and landlords who manage their own properties can have different motivations, priorities and approaches to managing a tenancy.

Agents make money from managing rental properties, not from owning them.

Given the fact it is landlords who decide whether to retain their services, the priority for agents will be keeping the business of the landlord, rather than retaining the tenant, especially in tight rental markets where vacancy rates are low.

Research in the United States has found a link between how a rental property is managed and the maintenance and security of the home.

For example, one study from Rochester, in the state of New York, found homes managed by agents were more likely to fall short of minimum housing standards than those managed by landlords.

Renting through an agent versus a landlord

So, does the same hold true in Australia? Our new research sought to find out.

Using the Australian Housing Conditions Dataset, a large-scale nationally representative survey which included over 12,000 households living in private rentals, we compared the experiences of renters renting directly from a landlord with those renting via an agent.

We compared reported renter experiences across three important aspects:

unjustified rent increases

delayed responses to maintenance requests

limitations in how the home is used — for example, restrictions on having pets or putting up pictures.

We focused on renters who had lived in their homes for at least a year and who had a formal lease agreement — excluding, for example, renting from friends or family without a formal agreement.

We found these issues were common.

Nearly one in five private renters said they had experienced an unjustified rent increase, nearly 29 per cent had experienced a restriction in how they used their home, and over one third had had a delay in repairs or maintenance.

But some renters were more likely to report these problems than others:

Source: The Conversation / Amy Clair / Sha Liu / Emma Baker

These differences remained when we adjusted for property type, household characteristics, and location.

Renters dealing with agents were 2.4 times as likely to report restrictions on how they use their homes, and 2.6 times more likely to report delayed repairs or unjustified rent increases.

Could better training and standards help?

Property agents can bring valuable expertise — including knowledge of tenancy law and systems for organising repairs.

However, as our results show, professional management does not automatically mean a better experience for renters.

Agents often manage many properties, relying on standard procedures that can leave less room for negotiation.

Renters who deal directly with landlords may have more opportunities to discuss decisions and negotiate arrangements that work for them. But some agencies discourage, even ban, direct contact between landlord and tenant.

READ MORE The Aussies who could be caught in the middle of the housing tax shake-up

For many landlords, using a property manager is convenient or necessary.

Better training for agents could improve the experience for tenants, and potentially for landlords too.

This could include skills in communicating with renters, resolving problems and understanding how management decisions affect people's ability to make a home.

Alongside clear standards and accountability, these skills could help agents meet their responsibilities to landlords while also supporting better experiences for renters.

Amy Clair is a Professor in Housing Policy at Adelaide University and the University of Essex. She receives funding from the Australian Research Council, the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute, and the United Kingdom Economic and Social Research Council.

Emma Baker is a Professor of Housing Research at Adelaide University and receives funding from the Australian Research Council, the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute, and the United Kingdom Economic and Social Research Council.

Sha Liu is a research fellow at the Australian Centre for Housing Research at Adelaide University and receives funding from the Australian Research Council.

title: Australians are the first to feel the impact of a growing global issue
text:
In Brief Two major global outages have been attributed to issues with system updates.

A popular time for system updates avoids the workday in the US and Europe, but impacts Australians instead.

Two of the biggest software outages in recent memory were caused, at least in part, by updates that went wrong. They also both set a cascade of failures in motion.

Administrators have traditionally tried to run updates during off-peak hours when people aren't online, so that if something goes wrong, the impact is minimised.

But when people all around the world working in different time zones rely on the technology, the impact is not necessarily minimised, but moved.

Last week's Microsoft outage brought emails and some calls to a stop for Australian users for nearly 24 hours and put a spotlight on how dependent the world is on a small number of global systems.

According to Dr Rahat Masood, a senior lecturer in computer science and engineering at UNSW, every company has its own rules to follow for managing updates.
