"Technology companies like Microsoft, they operate globally, but their systems and updates don't always follow the same schedule everywhere," she said.

"That means a problem that might go relatively unnoticed in one country, in United States, it can cause significant disruption in another, like in Australia."

The downside of universal time

In July 2024, the CrowdStrike outage sent the world into blue-tinted chaos.

Businesses, schools, airports, supermarkets and banks around the world faced an error known as the "blue screen of death" after an issue with a cybersecurity software triggered failures in millions of Microsoft Windows devices.

At the time, the company's CEO said the issue was caused by "a defect found in a single content update".

It all started with a configuration update released at 04:09 UTC.

UTC, or Coordinated Universal Time, is the world's standard for accurately establishing clocks and time zones worldwide. It's also often used in computing and digital infrastructure to avoid ambiguity.

While similar to Greenwich Mean Time, which is still observed as a time zone in some countries, UTC doesn't operate as its own time zone, and no country officially uses it as their local time.

Passengers at airports around the world were disrupted in the CrowdStrike outage. Source: AAP / Hindustan Times/Sipa USA

The timing of CrowdStrike's update was typical.

For example, Microsoft offers a guide for managing updates using planned maintenance windows in their training materials. Their default preset for maintenance is 01:00 to 04:00. 04:00 UTC is also the start of their recommended maintenance for North and South America.

In the US, many users have already wrapped up their working days, while those in Europe are preparing for theirs, leaving neither major market predominantly online.

But in Australia, and other areas in the Asia Pacific, it's the middle of the working day.

On one side of the country, the impacts of the CrowdStrike outage hit Sydney mid-afternoon, and on the other, Perth experienced it from the middle of the day.

Based on its positioning relative to the major markets of the US and Europe, Australia's time zones are more vulnerable to being among the first to feel the impacts when updates deployed around this period go wrong.

A Sunday evening window, such as that recommended by Microsoft for systems based in the US, might avoid local users experiencing potential issues. But Australian users beginning their work week would still feel it.

A canary in the Asia Pacific?

There are two key approaches to running updates for systems used across multiple countries: choosing a single slot where the change will apply everywhere according to UTC or following the sun to gradually release as each time zone hits a certain time in their local time zone.

Unfortunately, Australia doesn't tend to fare better under either of these approaches.

Australian and New Zealand workers are among the first to log on each day, giving them access to updates before other continents wake up to begin their day. It can also make them some of the first to experience the consequences of updates gone wrong.

"When one major platform fails, either Google or Microsoft, the consequences are far beyond their borders," Masood said.

When Microsoft was unable to resolve its outage before the end of the day in the US, Australian workers woke up to begin their working day without access to their emails, messages and files.

Masood said the outage highlighted global dependence on a small number of global technology providers.

"What we have seen on Friday is that when the email was not working, when SharePoint was not working, OneDrive was not working, Teams was not working properly, we noticed that we were stopped," she said.

"Australia was not ready for this type of outage for such a long period of time and there was no alternative backups for us available."

The lack of resilience to technological failures is also a chance to support local technological production rather than tech giants.

"Can we develop something that actually we can say that this is ours and we are not dependent on the other time zones?" she said.

In the meantime, the focus should be on ensuring changes are fully tested as technology gets more complicated.

"These companies really need to think about, if they're operating globally, do it in batches, do it gradually and then go for the whole thing."

"It's better to actually make an update gradually rather than making the disruption for the whole world."

title: Investigation launched after Melbourne Cup runner dumped in skip bin
text:
IN BRIEF So You Are's trainer said he was 'deeply distressed' at the handling of the athlete's remains.

The gelding was euthanised on Monday due to a severe bout of colic.

An equine hospital has apologised to So You Are's owners and trainer after the body of the 2026 Melbourne Cup runner was left in a skip bin at a local tip.

The five-year-old gelding's dumped body was filmed at Sydney's Cleanaway Lucas Heights Resource Recovery Centre, with the graphic footage posted to social media on Monday afternoon.

His trainer Bjorn Baker confirmed on Tuesday it was So You Are, who had to be euthanised on Monday due to a severe bout of colic.

"Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," the prominent conditioner said in a statement, adding he expected a full explanation of what had occurred.

"He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death."

Promising stayer So You Are took ill while at a spelling farm after finishing eighth in Australia's greatest race on November 3, a week after winning the Bendigo Cup.

He was rushed to REC Equine Specialists at Horsley Park in Sydney's west after showing signs of colic on Monday morning.

Surgery could not save the horse and he was euthanised under anaesthesia.

Racing NSW (RNSW) said its preliminary investigations found So You Are was being held temporarily awaiting burial when the footage was recorded.

"The way in which So You Are's body was left is distressing and completely unacceptable," the regulator said in a statement.

"So You Are deserved to be treated with dignity and respect.

"Under NSW Department of Primary Industries guidelines, a licensed landfill is the preferred option for animals who have died via euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process.

"That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner."

RNSW said if any wrongdoing was discovered in its ongoing investigation it would take "appropriate action".

REC Equine Specialists managing partner Jonathan Lumsden said he had spoken with So You Are's owners and trainer to personally apologise.

"He should have been promptly and respectfully buried," Lumsden said.

"What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone who cared for him.

"We are deeply sorry."

Lumsden pointed out the veterinary practice did not carry out the burial but acknowledged it chose the provider and arrangements, which were "not good enough" and "must change".

The practice has, effective immediately, stopped using the service provider involved and is reviewing how those it contracts care for horses after death, from collection to final burial.

Lumsden vowed to share their findings with So You Are's connections and RNSW.

"No owner should have to go through what So You Are's connections have experienced this week," Lumsden said.

"We will make sure it does not happen again."

Racing NSW is also reviewing its existing rules and minimum standards and has promised to work with the Department of Primary Industries on steps to avoid a repeat.

Baker added his thoughts remained with So You Are's owner-breeder Stuart Ramsey and family and with all the stable's staff, "for whom this has compounded an already devastating loss".

title: What we know about the planned Rwanda migrant deportation centre
text:
In brief The initiative was taken by Austria, Germany, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands.

Nationals of any country are eligible, according to those involved in the plan.

Five European Union (EU) countries overnight announced a plan to establish a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda, the first such facility outside the bloc.

Here is what we know about the "return-hub" initiative by Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands.

Who will be deported and how?

The five nations have been exploring sending migrants to centres outside Europe for months, with the pilot project planned to be launched next year.

During a joint press announcement in Vienna, ministers from the five EU countries and Rwanda remained evasive on the project's scope.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

But according to people involved, the centre will house around 100 migrants.

They will be men and women whose asylum applications have been rejected but who refuse to return to their countries of origin, despite having exhausted all avenues of appeal.

According to those involved in the plan, nationals of any country will be eligible to be sent to the facility, although minors would be excluded.

National authorities from the five European countries' national authorities will be responsible for transferring rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda.

Non-governmental refugee and humanitarian organisations are worried the initiative could ultimately target all asylum seekers — a claim denied by the five countries involved.

What conditions will migrants face in Rwanda?

Once they arrive in Rwanda, authorities of the east African country will take charge of them, and they will receive residence permits.

They will be placed in a centre, which Rwandan authorities referred to as a "welcome centre".

The five European countries insist that it will be open, without any deprivation of liberty or barbed wire.

READ MORE Tony Burke announces backpacker visa backdown after industry pressure

A site has already been identified. The European countries, however, have refused to specify where it is.

They only stress that it is not one of the centres the United Kingdom had planned to use.

London had announced plans in 2022 to send asylum seekers to Rwanda, but the project was ultimately abandoned because of legal obstacles.

How long will the migrants stay at the centre?

The idea is for the migrants to stay in the centre for a few months, with the aim that they then integrate into Rwandan society.

"These illegal migrants who will be relocated to Rwanda are not going to be kept in a camp or in a dedicated area. They will be integrated in our society," Rwandan interior minister Vincent Biruta told the press conference in Vienna.

Vocational training and language courses are to be offered to them.

The five EU countries also say an independent monitoring mechanism — the details of which have not been spelled out — will be put in place to ensure respect for human rights.

Another option is for the exiles to return voluntarily to their country of origin, but not to the EU.

Is the move legal?

Those involved in the plan hope it will discourage migrants from trying to settle on the European continent, besides getting those asylum seekers whose applications have been rejected out of the EU.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the project aimed to send a "signal ... that you can no longer enter the European Union illegally and think that you can just stay around".

The EU states have refused to say what Rwanda would receive in return.

The five countries claim that the legal basis is solid, relying on relevant EU legislation adopted a few months ago.

They have dismissed fierce criticism and concern about the treatment of migrants.

The plans are expected to face court challenges.

title: One Nation, Greens weigh in after Qld and NT reject medical guidance on puberty blockers
text:
In Brief National advice has recommended puberty blockers as a possible part of treatment for young trans people under several conditions.

Public hospitals in both Queensland and the NT are prohibited from prescribing puberty blockers to children under 18.

New advice from Australia's independent medical council recommending puberty blockers for teenage trans and gender diverse people, in limited cases, will be ignored in Queensland and the Northern Territory, and One Nation says it will not support the treatment nationally or if elected in Victoria.

Meanwhile, the federal government, Opposition and Greens all welcomed the advice.

The National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) released interim advice on Monday that, as part of a shared decision between a young person, their parents or carers, and their doctors, puberty blockers can be considered if the young person has reached puberty and is assessed as suitable. The treatment is reversible.

Health Minister Mark Butler told Channel Nine on Tuesday that the public debate concerned a relatively small group of very vulnerable young people who are over-represented in mental health and suicide statistics.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

He argued that the issue should be referred to the Australian health and medical research body "rather than have debate settled by commentators in our big newspapers".

Butler also defended the research behind the guidelines, which found a low level of certainty for better mental health outcomes for trans and gender diverse teenagers who accessed puberty blockers.

"It's not unusual to have guidelines indicate a level of low certainty around evidence. More recently, I've seen that in pregnancy care guidelines, dementia care guidelines, arthritis, and even stroke management as well," Butler said.

Equality Australia welcomed the guidance on Monday, with CEO Anna Brown saying it "reinforces that the care trans young people are receiving in Australia today is grounded in evidence, informed by clinical expertise and guided by the individual needs of young people".

Why have Queensland and the NT rejected the guidance?

The Queensland and Northern Territory governments immediately rejected the NHMRC advice on Monday, insisting they will maintain their bans based on their own reviews of the evidence.

Queensland Health Minister Tim Nicholls said the state had already conducted its own independent review and that the NHMRC's advice won't change its decision.

The state introduced a ban on public hospitals prescribing any gender-affirming hormone treatments in January 2025, following research in the United Kingdom by paediatrician Hilary Cass.

The Cass review of youth gender identity services in the UK found the international and local evidence base supporting early puberty suppression for minors with gender dysphoria or gender incongruence is "remarkably weak" and lacked long-term data on clinical effectiveness or safety.

READ MORE Kyro wanted gender-affirming treatment but was told he had to wait to make the decision

Butler said Queensland's own review didn't have the status, scope, or "purpose" of the council, and the UK review was influenced by "questionable private prescribing practices" that do not occur in Australia.

The biggest local gender clinic, in Melbourne, prescribed puberty blockers to an average of eight young people over eight years, with wait times for treatment averaging 530 days, Butler said.

Nicholls said the state's position "remains unchanged and we will continue to prioritise the health, safety and wellbeing of young Queenslanders".

Queensland's ban was briefly overturned by the Supreme Court last year, but Nicholls used ministerial powers to immediately reinstate it hours after the court's decision.

The NT government also said in a statement that its ban will remain in place.

A spokesperson for the Northern Territory government told Nine Newspapers that its decision is consistent with those of Queensland, the United Kingdom and Finland, "which have all taken a cautious approach".

Labor ordered the NHMRC review into the prescription of gender-affirming hormones for young people two days after the Queensland government's 2025 ban.

The new guidelines do not require a child to be diagnosed with gender dysphoria, which is psychological distress caused when someone's gender identity does not align with the sex they were assigned at birth.

What have others said?

Greens leader David Shoebridge told SBS News Australia should be taking the best advice from the best experts.

"This seems like a very credible policy that's been considered not by politicians who are trying to make a political point, but by the medical experts," Shoebridge said. "I think the more we listen to the medical and ethical experts, and the less we listen to the likes of the NT chief minister or the Queensland premier in this space, the more the country will be on the right track."

Liberal senator Andrew Bragg told Channel Nine on Tuesday the transgender community should not be used as a "political football".

"I think there are people in politics who've used them [as] part of their kind of hate campaign," Bragg said. "They are a tiny minority, and we should be kind to one another. We've got to live and let live ethos in this country."

The senator said decisions about gender-affirming treatment were, for the most part, "not judgements children should be making", but said there were rare circumstances in which accessing puberty blockers would be appropriate for a child's health.

A One Nation spokesperson said it would fight to ban the treatment if elected in Victoria or federally.

The federal Coalition noted the new advice deviates from the UK Cass review and does not require a gender dysphoria diagnosis.

The advice is open for public comment until 18 January, with clinical guidelines, beyond the use of puberty suppressants, developed "probably into 2028", Butler said.

title: Tony Burke announces backpacker visa backdown after industry pressure
text:
In brief Labor announced a plan earlier this year to significantly reduce third-year working holiday visas to 5,000.

Tony Burke says that figure will now be 25,000, while extending regional work requirements for second-year working holidaymakers.

After viral videos, threats of harvests being left to wither and fears from the Labor backbench, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has agreed to some concessions over his backpacker visa crackdown.

Despite announcing a major reduction for third-year working holiday visas to just 5,000 earlier this year, Burke has announced Labor will lift that number to 25,000.

Those who are successful will still be chosen through a ballot system.

"These changes give businesses and working holidaymakers clear rules and time to plan, while making sure the program continues to support the regions and industries that rely on it," Burke told reporters in Cairns on Tuesday.

"Australia will continue to welcome working holidaymakers. These reforms make the program fairer, more targeted and sustainable for the long term."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The minister is claiming a win in the compromise deal, extending the second-year regional work requirements for the visa from three months to four months.

From March, the number of days working holidaymakers will need to complete in the regions to be eligible for a second year will increase from 88 to 120.

"This creates a very significant shift, but also means for the people who are wanting to qualify for their second year, we're getting more regional days out of them," Burke said.

Burke announced a raft of migration changes, including the backpacker move, in his address to the National Press Club in September, following delays and concerns from inside Labor.

READ MORE Why fixing Australia's immigration system is not just about cutting migrants

Labor MPs in regional areas of the Northern Territory and Queensland have also been facing direct lobbying about the threat of a diminishing workforce.

Labor backbencher Matt Smith said on Tuesday he had led a delegation of Far North Queensland industry leaders to Canberra to help "guide the shape of those reforms".

Burke targeted the backpacker numbers as part of his attempt to ensure the government doesn't overshoot its net overseas migration (NOM) targets.

The NOM has become a major focus of political attacks from One Nation and the Opposition, which have accused the government of failing to manage migration and allowing numbers to balloon without adequate housing.

Coalition urges Labor to 'axe' ballot

Following Burke's announcement, Opposition leader Angus Taylor criticised the government's proposed ballot system for second and third-year working holiday visas.

"They should just axe it," Taylor told reporters in Townsville, adding that the Coalition would "absolutely" repeal the system if elected.

Burke said the Opposition's proposed immigration policy — which would remove caps on second and third-year working holiday visas — would cut temporary migration numbers without affecting "the areas where they are really needed".

The government says the changes announced on Tuesday won’t affect the overall NOM projections, which Labor wants to bring down from 245,000 this financial year to 225,000 next year.

Australia is still negotiating with the United Kingdom over changing the free trade deal that has exempted British working holidaymakers from working in regional areas.

Burke said discussions are underway to reach an agreement with the UK that would mean a "different sort of obligation than what is currently there for UK backpackers" and said talks had been promising.

title: Fake websites, fraudulent listings: The tactics scammers are using to target travellers
text:
In brief The government's travel advisory website says scams can affect travellers at every stage of their journey.

Common travel-related scams include fake visa and entry requirement websites.

Smartraveller has issued a warning to Australians ahead of the holiday season, with scammers looking to take advantage of tourists.

The government's travel advisory website said scams can affect travellers at every stage of their journey, including when researching destinations, booking flights and accommodation, and while travelling domestically or overseas.

It said scammers are getting increasingly better at making their scams look legitimate.

"They may pretend to be an airline, airport, accommodation provider, travel business or government agency," Smartraveller said, noting that scammers will set up fake websites, emails, text messages and social media accounts.

Common travel-related scams include: fake visa and entry requirement websites, fraudulent accommodation listings or travel bookings, suspicious booking changes and messages claiming to be from airlines, airports, accommodation or government agencies.

"The scammer operated a convincing website and offered a 'free digital travel assistant service'," according to an update from the consumer watchdog.

title: 'A dream come true': The next James Bond has been revealed
text:
After months of speculation, British actor Robert Pattinson was overnight named as the new James Bond, stepping into the coveted role of the world's most famous fictional spy.

"Amazon MGM Studios have announced that Robert Pattinson will take on the iconic role of James Bond," the studio said.

Pattinson, 40, will succeed Daniel Craig as the super-suave MI6 agent, "ushering in a new era for one of cinema's most celebrated characters", the studio added.

The choice of the Batman actor received immediate royal approval, with the British monarchy's social media accounts sharing the announcement with the comment: "Welcome to His Majesty's Secret Service, Mr Bond."

It will be the first 007 film since long-term producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael Wilson stepped back and Amazon took creative control of the franchise, after acquiring the series' parent company MGM.

title: The 'missing piece' in Australia's fight against an enduring addiction
text:
in brief The number of illicit tobacco products has dropped, while the number of smokers continues to fall.

Experts and advocates say there needs to be a shift in the retail environment to further reduce smoking and illegal products.

Australia's illicit tobacco market has shrunk for the first time in years, according to new government data. However, experts say the crackdown is missing a crucial measure: restricting where tobacco products can be sold.

Data from the Illicit Tobacco and E-cigarette Commission (ITEC) has revealed a 24 per cent drop in the volume of contraband product in circulation over the past financial year.

While the exact size of the black-market sector cannot be calculated, it is estimated to have shrunk by as much as 1,438 tonnes.

It follows five years of significant growth in the amount of illegal tobacco available on the market.

At the same time, there has been a downward trend in the number of Australians smoking, but of those who do use tobacco, a growing number are using illicit products.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Becky Freeman, a tobacco control expert at the University of Sydney, said the data suggests a "changing of the tide" in the fight against illicit tobacco, but that more needs to be done.

Freeman said the widespread availability of cigarettes and vapes at supermarkets and convenience stores contributed to the use of both illicit and legal tobacco products.

Tobacco use carries serious health risks and is a leading cause of preventable illness and death.

"We’ve never questioned that this deadly product should just be sold absolutely everywhere in every single community all across the country. And to me, that’s the missing piece that could really tackle this issue," she told SBS News.

READ MORE The dramatic shift in a longstanding Australian addiction

By reducing the availability of cigarettes, it could lead to fewer people taking up smoking to begin with, who may go on to later buy illicit tobacco products.

Vendors must hold a valid state or territory tobacco licence for each physical premises or online store where tobacco or non-tobacco smoking products are sold.

Illicit tobacco on the decline, government says, as excise revenue falls

ITEC estimates the total volume of black-market tobacco has fallen to 5,893 tonnes and could be as low as 4,453 tonnes.

Source: SBS News

The government said the decline was due to stronger enforcement, larger seizures, and better coordination among federal, state and territory agencies.

But Freeman said enforcement is only one part of the solution to stopping the illicit tobacco trade.

She told SBS News that the product is too easy to access, with smokers able to go to a convenience store "with ease" and pay less for an illicit product than for an approved one.

"It's your local friendly shopkeeper who will sell you these products. And so they just kind of go, 'oh, well, you know, they're willing to sell them to me. It can't be that bad.'"

'No time to ease up'

The decline in black market tobacco products, combined with fewer smokers, is welcome news to the Australian Council of Smoking and Health (ACOSH).

Its CEO Laura Hunter told SBS News the government should continue to ramp up its efforts to stop the illicit trade.

Source: SBS News

"We need to keep disrupting the trade at every point in the supply chain. We need to disrupt it before it reaches Australia, at the border, and in the communities where it's sold," she said.

"It's no time to ease up."

Addressing the "retail environment" around where tobacco is sold is key, she added, saying "there is an incredibly high number of tobacco retailers".

Australia has around 40,000 retailers that are selling tobacco products legally, according to ACOSH.

The country has about 9,500 supermarkets and roughly 7,000 petrol stations, meaning tobacco is far more widely available than everyday grocery or fuel items.

SBS News asked the federal government whether it would consider restricting which vendors could sell tobacco products, given the number of vendors compared to supermarkets and petrol stations.

Staff for Assistant Customs Minister Julian Hill pointed to a speech he delivered in March.

"That imbalance raises questions about whether tobacco products should instead be sold only through mixed‑use retail settings, subject to stricter licensing, oversight and compliance. Interesting questions for the future," Hill said in an excerpt.

Retail licensing of tobacco falls solely within the remit of states and territories.

The missing piece in combating tobacco

Freeman argued that reducing the number of vendors permitted to sell tobacco products could curb the sale of illicit cigarettes and vapes.

"Tobacco shops are literally everywhere. Any sort of store can sell you cigarettes," she said.

"And to really get on top of this issue, we have got to start ramping that down. We need fewer places selling cigarettes, which would help with enforcement efforts as well."

Source: SBS News

Coral Gartner, a tobacco control expert at the University of Queensland, agreed that the tobacco product supply chain needs stronger governance.

"This is a really harmful product that's addictive. And the way that it's been allowed to be sold in stores is not the way that we regulate other harmful addictive products," she told SBS News.

Gartner said that health campaigns around the dangers of smoking have been effective in reducing smoking rates. However, she wants to see more support for cessation programs.

"In Queensland they've got some great programs where if you meet certain criteria, you can get free nicotine replacement therapy sent to you, along with support counselling," she said.

Gartner wants to see programs like that rolled out permanently nationwide.

Tobacco excise revenue, a tax on tobacco products, fell to about $4.1 billion in the 2026 financial year, down sharply from a record high of $16.3 billion in 2020.

Meanwhile, the government reported that the illicit tobacco trade cost between $7.7 billion and $11.8 billion in potential revenue in the 2024–2025 financial year alone.

"This reduces revenue that can fund the public health system in treating smoking-related illnesses," the Combatting Illicit Tobacco Bill 2026 reads.

title: 'I will carry it in my heart': This Aboriginal teenager has made surfing history
text:
IN BRIEF Leihani Zoric has won the ISA Open World Surfing Champion in Peru.

The Byron Bay local is the first Aboriginal person to win a world surfing championship.

Australian Leihani Zoric is surfing's new star, making history at 14 as the sport's youngest world champion.

The national Irukandjis team had a massive day at the International Surfing Association world games in Peru, qualifying an extra third spot for the women at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.

Ethan Ewing also won the men's world title as Australia claimed the team category for the second straight year and the seventh time overall.

Zoric's win came 10 days after her 14th birthday. The Yued teenager is the first Australian Indigenous surfer to win a world championship.

In September, she also became the youngest surfer to win an under-18 junior world championship.

title: A plan to keep more of Australia's gas onshore faces a constitutional problem
text:
In brief Labor's gas reservation plan faces Senate roadblocks over design, WA inclusion and ministerial powers.

Coalition, Greens and crossbench have opposed the bill over investment risks, tax demands and climate concerns.

The Albanese government wants to push down gas prices by engineering a "modest oversupply" of gas but a proposed reservation scheme is deadlocked in the Senate due to disagreements over its design.

The proposed rules to force liquefied natural gas (LNG) exporters to pump more gas to Australians are problematic for the industry, the Coalition and the Greens said, for different reasons, including whether they encourage or discourage new supply.

The government needs the backing of either the Greens or the Coalition to pass the bill, as manufacturing unions urge the Senate to pass it before the end of the year.

The laws would create a Domestic Supply Obligation (DSO) to force big LNG exporters to reserve and supply up to 20 per cent of their annual export energy to Australians as calculated by the Australian Energy Regulator (AER), starting in 2028.

The AER will forecast domestic demand, add a 10 per cent market oversupply buffer, subtract non-exporter supply, and spread the remaining amount across LNG exporters.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Resources Minister Madeleine King said the policy will shield households, gas-powered electricity generators, and local manufacturers from international price spikes and domestic shortfalls.

A national scheme, with a single-state exception

For the law to be constitutional, it must apply to all states, but Australia has two disconnected gas markets. Western Australia's pipelines don't connect to the east coast because they don't run across the Great Sandy Desert and the Nullarbor Plain.

King acknowledged the issue and said the law allows DSO for the Western Australian market to be set at zero, or very low levels.

The Coalition and WA gas industry want a carve-out from the rules but Labor is only allowing adjustments through a ministerial decision. King argued that including WA helps make the scheme constitutionally robust.

Opposition leader Angus Taylor told reporters on Monday: "Our position is very clear that WA shouldn't be in it because they don't have the problem we have on the east coast".

"We do not need WA being part of this scheme," Taylor said. "WA says that. The WA premier says that, so sort it out. It's pretty simple."

Grattan Energy and Climate Change deputy program director Hamish McKenzie told SBS News that a WA parliamentary inquiry found exporters were "significantly under-delivering gas".

READ MORE Australian gas giant and Traditional Owners locked in $300 million compensation battle

"The brutal reality is that the state gas reservation in WA is full of holes," McKenzie said.

"The federal scheme is much, much stronger, and if it was applied in WA, it would probably result in substantially more of West Australia's gas being kept onshore for West Australian users.

"Gas producers don't want that, and they are running a campaign to make sure that WA is exempt."

Ministerial powers queried

The minister's power to reduce or exclude gas companies' obligations from the scheme is controversial because one of the three east coast exporters — Gladstone LNG — has signed contracts to export much more gas than its planned production until at least 2036.

If a company's obligations under the new law require them to break an export contract and if they take "active steps" to try to deliver domestic gas, they may be excused.

"The minister of the day has a huge amount of discretion as to how they will implement the reservation," McKenzie said.

There aren't a lot of guardrails around the minister's ability to dictate supply and waive obligations, he said.

"The thing that should really be fixed is probably not the fine details of how it will be applied, but the circumstances in which the minister can actually use that discretion."

Stuffing a golden gas goose with oversupply?

The minister can set an "oversupply" percentage, between 0 and 10 per cent of demand, which is the "biggest problem with the legislation", McKenzie said.

"Forcing 10 per cent more supply into the market than is demanded every year risks massively tanking the price, putting unviable pressure on domestic gas producers in a way that could, after a couple of years, leave the east coast gas market even more reliant on the exported sea gas supply, which is actually the opposite of what the reservation is trying to do," he said.

Taylor told reporters on Monday that to get prices down, you need more supply, and you won't have more supply if you trash the industry.

"So, they will push too much supply into the [Australian] market, but we need investment," Taylor said.

"We need to see a price that's going to get the investment, as well as the price to consumers, industrial and household, small business. That is achievable whilst we're still getting the investment."

Australia must produce more gas, not simply shuffle existing supplies around, Opposition resources spokesperson senator Susan McDonald said.

"Labor’s proposal in its current form will drive away investment, destroy domestic-only producers, discourage new production and ultimately leave Australians with less gas and higher prices.

No reservations for the Greens or crossbench

The Greens won't support the bill unless it includes a 25 per cent tax on gas exports. Greens senator Steph Hodgins-May said the government should "do a deal for everyday Australians, not for gas donors", warning the new law may make it easier to open new gas fields and "make the climate crisis worse".

Independent senator David Pocock said Australia "needed a better return for its exports" and continues to push for a 25 per cent tax.

"I think it’s a good start, but I’m going to continue to push for a fair return for all Australians and for future generations of Australians on a resource that, once it’s sold, is gone," he told Channel Nine on Monday.

"We’ve got to get better at capturing long-term benefit from the sale of our resources."

King has rejected this, saying nothing gets cheaper after it's taxed.

"We have seen other countries where they do introduce what Senator Pocock has suggested, like a windfall tax, and what that has ended up doing is driving the industry basically away."

title: What Anthony Albanese's fried chicken move could signal to the world
text:
In brief Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has celebrated the upcoming launch of Filipino fast food chain Jollibee in Australia.

Some social media users expressed confusion about a video the prime minister posted supporting the chain.

While Anthony Albanese's promotion of a Filipino fast food chain has raised some eyebrows online, experts say the prime minister's fried chicken meal could strengthen ties with a regional ally.

Filipino fast food giant Jollibee is set to open in Australia — and the prime minister has celebrated the move in Manila with the company's president and CEO Ernesto Tanmantiong.

The chain, well-known in the Philippines for its fried chicken, operates more than 1,600 stores worldwide and aims to open 35 in NSW and Victoria over five years.

The Australian outlets are expected to create 900 direct jobs.

Albanese, who is in Manila for the summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), said he wants to see "more businesses choose Australia as a place to grow and succeed".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

He welcomed Jollibee as a "great example of the cultural connections that strengthen our relationship with the Philippines".

More than 400,000 people living in Australia were born in the Philippines, making it the country's fifth-largest diaspora community.

In a video posted to Albanese's Instagram, the prime minister celebrated with Jollibee staff and ate a meal at the fast food chain.

Concern about the PM's post

However, some social media users expressed confusion about the post and Albanese's endorsement of the chain, with one user commenting, "So, are you getting paid for this? Thought it was AI when I first saw it and can't believe it's for real."

Comedian and media personality Ben Sorensen commented on Albanese's video asking: "Was this a sponsored post?"

Politicians highlighting small businesses and large employers around Australia during election periods is extremely common, according to Emily Foley, a research fellow at the University of Canberra.

However, Foley told SBS News she hasn't seen this in a foreign affairs context before.

"I wouldn't say it's particularly common," she said.

Anne Nalder, founder and CEO of the Small Business Association of Australia, told SBS News the prime minister's promotion of Jollibee was "disappointing" at a time when small businesses in the food industry are "barely surviving" due to high costs.

Nalder also noted that around a third of small businesses in Australia are run by migrants.

"There's nothing wrong with an overseas company coming into Australia ... the thing about it is, I would like to see [the prime minister] concentrating on supporting Australian businesses because they need all the support they can get," she said.

A political calculation

Foley said there aren't any rules for politicians that would restrict a post like Albanese's, and his decision to post it likely comes down to a political calculation about appealing to Australia's Filipino diaspora.

"There is a bit of a grappling about what is acceptable for politicians to put on social media and the public sphere, but I don't think there's anything in particular that's necessarily frowned upon [in this case]," Foley said.

Whilst attracting critical comments, Albanese's video also received many supportive responses and attracted over 71,000 likes.

This is also not the first time the prime minister has encouraged a foreign business to enter Australia. During a meeting in the United Arab Emirates in 2025, Albanese visited a Lulu Hypermarket store — one of the largest retail chains in the Middle East, with over 250 stores across the region.

Albanese said at the time he had a discussion with Lulu Hypermarket chair Yusuff Ali as they walked around the store and invited the company to bring more competition to Australia's supermarket sector.

"They are the largest throughout the Middle East. Egypt, here ... the second-largest in Saudi Arabia," Albanese said.

"We know that Aldi, of course, has come to Australia, but this is a significant player that has an engagement with Australia, and I want to see that competition."

However, no plans have been announced for Lulu Hypermarket to enter the Australian market.

Fried chicken diplomacy

On Sunday, the Philippines and Australia signed a defence pact, strengthening ties between the two nations, which have grown over the past decade.

The agreement will step up maritime training and activities amid shared security concerns about China's growing militarisation of the South China Sea, particularly in an area deemed part of Filipino territorial waters by a UN arbitration in 2016.

Australia has taken part in 12 joint patrols with the Philippines in the South China Sea, with four in the last year.

However, Albanese insisted the defence agreement was not aimed specifically at any one country.

"This is about supporting the sovereignty of every country," he said.

READ MORE Australia to ink Philippines defence pact before Quad meeting with Donald Trump

While supporting the fried chicken chain is a demonstration of softer diplomacy than a defence pact, emeritus professor Paul Hutchcroft told SBS News the prime minister was likely trying to forge a connection between Australia and the Philippines.

"Jollibee is a source of pride for many Filipinos, competing successfully at home with American fast-food chains while also expanding overseas," he said.

"I can imagine that the PM was tapping into that sense of pride as a way of connecting with citizens of an important Australian ally."

Foley said Albanese's support of Jollibee has "interesting" foreign affairs implications as it highlights a "non-US, non-Western style business that's coming into Australia".

"It obviously speaks to the Labor government's real focus on trying to engage more with the Indo-Pacific, in particular highlighting things like ASEAN centrality — the kind of push to focus more on the political, economic and social ties and connections with neighbouring regional partners, rather than necessarily with the US."

title: What Coles shoppers need to know about the cyber attack on the retailer
text:
IN BRIEF Coles was the target of a cyber attack on Monday, but says no customer data was compromised.

The retailer recommended online shoppers update and strengthen their passwords as the hack is investigated.

Australia's second-largest supermarket chain has urged customers to take basic online precautions after it was targeted in a cyber attack.

Coles revealed it was investigating a cyber security incident on Monday morning but said there was no evidence that any data was compromised.

Coles is also investigating reported issues with Liquorland's click-and-collect service.

"We have not identified any evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed from Coles' systems," Coles said in a statement.

The supermarket giant asked customers to continue to be wary of scams as investigations continue.

"We advise everyone to take basic online precautions and recommend remaining vigilant to suspicious links, attempts to solicit personal information ... and potential scam activity," a customer notice said.

"Coles will never ask you to provide your password or other sensitive account information through an unsolicited email or SMS."

The retailer said shoppers were able to shop as normal both in store and online.

The grocer apologised to its customers for any concerns they might have at "a time of increasing cyber incidents in Australia and around the world".

Madison Huang was yelling. Her father, Nvidia’s chief executive Jensen Huang, had been scheduled to headline a conference in New Delhi in February. Shortly before the event, he pulled out and tapped a longtime lieutenant, Jay Puri, to attend instead. But Nvidia hadn’t buttoned up its plans for the conference, infuriating Madison Huang. On a call before the event, she berated other employees — including Puri — for being unprepared, said three people familiar with the meeting. Eventually, Puri interrupted and told her he could answer her questions if she stopped yelling at him. Less than six months later, Puri left his role at Nvidia. Madison Huang, senior director of product marketing at Nvidia, attends the 2026 World Robot Conference in Beijing. Reuters The tense meeting highlighted the powerful and sometimes disruptive role Huang, 35, played at the company her father co-founded, according to more than a dozen current and former employees who spoke on condition of anonymity about the family’s leadership of Nvidia. Before Jensen Huang resigned last week, Madison had become his de facto chief of staff, with considerable authority over more seasoned executives. That influence creates an immediate challenge for Colette Kress, Nvidia’s interim chief executive, who replaced Huang. Kress must quickly determine how much power Madison Huang will have in the company after her father’s exit. She must also decide what to do about Jensen Huang’s other family members employed at the company: son, Spencer Huang, and son-in-law, Nico Caprez.

Huang resigned after revelations he had extramarital relationships with an Nvidia executive and a customer that US intelligence concluded was working for Chinese intelligence. The presence of Madison Huang has raised concerns among senior executives that she has conflicted loyalties between the company and her father. Those concerns were heightened over the last few days as Jensen Huang’s allies in Silicon Valley and on Wall Street started a campaign to reinstate him, and President Donald Trump said he “would not mind” if Huang returned to his job. ‘Nepotism is almost always a bad idea. There are few examples of it even working modestly well.’ Harvard Business School professor David Yoffie The Huang family, including Jensen, Madison and Spencer, and Puri did not respond to requests for comment. Jensen Huang, who employees say also has a hot temper, was aware of his daughter’s behaviour. He occasionally threatened to unleash an angry Madison Huang on other employees and told them to be afraid of her, said two people familiar with the comments. And even senior executives thought they could not disagree with her because of her direct line to the boss.

“Nepotism is almost always a bad idea,” said David Yoffie, a Harvard Business School professor who has served on more than a dozen corporate boards. “There are few examples of it even working modestly well.” Jensen Huang has said he wasn’t around much as a father. On a podcast recorded in April, he said he “missed a lot” of Madison and Spencer’s childhoods, including “all of their karate tournaments.” Jensen Huang’s wife, Lori, an accomplished electrical engineer, left her job to raise their children shortly before he co-founded Nvidia in 1993. Jensen Huang’s children Madison and Spencer are both Nvidia executives. Getty His children learned from an early age to care about Nvidia. “Both kids have read every shareholder letter, gone to every shareholder meeting, been to every single conference that I’ve ever done,” Jensen Huang said on the podcast. “Despite the fact that I was gone a lot, they found a way to always love the company.”

Advertisement

Huang’s children took winding paths to Nvidia. Madison received her bachelor’s degree from the Culinary Institute of America in 2012 and studied at Le Cordon Bleu in Paris and London from 2013 to 2015, according to her LinkedIn profile. She then managed luxury hotels and an Italian pastry shop owned by Louis Vuitton Moet Hennessy for four years. In 2019, she started at London Business School and then joined the family business in 2020. Related Article Opinion

He then owned a bar in Taipei, Taiwan, for eight years. In 2022, he joined Nvidia, where he is a director of product management for its robotics efforts. He is considered to be quiet and focused on his responsibilities, said seven people familiar with his work. Caprez, who met Madison Huang at London Business School, joined Nvidia in 2024 and became heavily involved in dealmaking. He has had a meteoric rise and is now a vice president of artificial intelligence infrastructure growth. He had attended executive team meetings with Jensen Huang. The trio has been viewed as an extension of Huang, but Madison has had the most influence. Colleagues have called her smart and a gifted marketer. She is officially a senior director of product marketing for physical AI. She has been known for having sharp insight, getting work done and being a polished representative of the company publicly.

But in practice, she has acted as a chief of staff for her father and had significant sway over Nvidia’s marketing and communications. She also joined his quarterly meetings with his executive team and helped build her father’s celebrity image. Interim chief executive Colette Kress must quickly determine how much power Madison Huang will have in the company after her father’s exit. About six years ago, Nvidia started marketing itself with a cartoon version of Jensen Huang, internally called “Toy Jensen.” After Madison Huang joined the company she pushed its marketing team to use that image of her father more widely, said two people familiar with the discussions. Nvidia started making pins with Toy Jensen and welcoming hires with a video of the cartoon. But Toy Jensen unnerved some employees, who worried it made Nvidia seem like a cult. In March, at its developer conference, Nvidia sold a $US178 sweater with Toy Jensen on it. Jensen Huang ended his keynote speech at the conference with a nearly four-minute-long video of his cartoon self singing at a campfire with robots.

Madison aggressively promoted and protected her father. The shocking image of the horse which she rode in the Melbourne Cup 15 days ago laying in a skip bin a day after his death was too distressing for jockey Rachel King to discuss. Kerrin McEvoy, a three-time Melbourne Cup winning jockey who, like King, cares for retired racehorses, called on the powers that be to make sure it doesn’t happen again after responsibility seemed to have been “shuffled down the pecking order”. So You Are, ridden by Rachel King, on its way to the barriers before competing in the Melbourne Cup at Flemington earlier this month. Racing Photos via Getty Images Trainer Joe Pride said it was sad the mistake of a few had reflected on a racing industry that typically treated horses so much better. The footage of So You Are in a skip bin at the Cleanaway Lucas Heights Resource Recovery Centre in southern Sydney on Tuesday sparked outrage and cast a pall over the metropolitan race meeting at Warwick Farm on Wednesday.

Advertisement

The five-year-gelding, which won $1.4 million in prizemoney, had been trained at the track by Bjorn Baker over the previous four months – a stint which included four wins, three with King aboard, as they surged through the ranks to make the $10 million Melbourne Cup on November 3 at Flemington. So You Are, owned by Scone breeder Stuart Ramsey, finished eighth and was recovering from his campaign in a paddock in Camden when he fell ill with a severe bout of colic. He was rushed to Randwick Equine Centre but could not be saved. Jockey Kerrin McEvoy. Flavio Brancaleone The image, shot by a builder, of So You Are in the bin after being humanely euthanised has rocked the racing industry and brought a wave of criticism on the code on social media. Cleanaway said the horse had been taken to its facility in a small tipper truck and placed in the skip bin before burial because it was unsafe for that vehicle to approach the landfill.

Advertisement

McEvoy, president of the NSW Jockeys Association, said it was “a really sad situation” that needed action to ensure it was never repeated. So You Are was found dumped in a skip bin at Lucas Heights in Sydney. Facebook “Any horse deserves better than that and it’s disappointing the way it unfolded for the horse and connections,” McEvoy said. “The responsibility looks as though it’s been shuffled down the pecking order and unfortunately the boxes haven’t been ticked off. The horses deserve better. It’s shocking. “I think we’re very good at [horse welfare], but there’s obviously areas that need to be improved and let’s just hope the powers above make sure that happens. It’s really disappointing.”

Advertisement

Pride, who also trains at Warwick Farm, said the treatment of the So You Are was a horrific situation. Related Article Opinion

Horse racing The disposal of So You Are has shocked the racing industry just as much as the public Kim Waugh Australian horse trainer “So many people are going to be held responsible for the actions of so few,” Pride said. “I don’t know how this happened. It’s clearly a mistake of some kind. An error of judgement, but it’s sad that it reflects upon all of racing because it’s nowhere near an indication of how we treat horses. “At the end of the day, the poor animal is dead, but there’s not much dignity there for it.”

King declined to comment, adding that talking about the incident would only make her cry. The disturbing discovery adds to a dark time for NSW racing after the death of 22-year-old Scone apprentice Izzy Neale following a race fall at Warren on November 8. Her mount Marnoo was euthanised because of a catastrophic injury.

Broken Hill Gold is set to spin out its Queensland gold assets into the soon-to-be-listed Manda Resources, which has just lodged a prospectus to raise $26.5 million in an initial public offering (IPO). The move will see Broken Hill’s followers receive a free distribution of shares in the new float and a priority offer to subscribe for more, crystallising the value of the 1.33-million-ounce Queensland portfolio, while leaving the parent company to focus on its burgeoning South Australian copper-gold ground. Broken Hill Gold’s demerged Queensland gold assets are set to join the new Manda Resources IPO, in a value-unlocking event for existing shareholders. Notably, Manda has also attracted the backing of multi-billion-dollar gold producer Emerald Resources, which will provide $5.24 million in backing to the planned IPO and emerge as one of the company’s major shareholders. Subject to approvals, Broken Hill will distribute the 64 million Manda shares to be listed at 50c, via an in-specie distribution at a ratio of one Manda share for every 8.40 Broken Hill Gold shares held at the end of this year.

Advertisement

‘This is an important value-creation event for Broken Hill Gold shareholders.’ Broken Hill Gold managing director Matthew Boyes The transaction will see Broken Hill’s Alice River gold and St George gold-antimony projects leave the stable and join Territory Minerals’ Tregoora, Northcote, Atric and Reedy gold projects, with the broader Australian market seeing renewed interest in dedicated gold spin-outs. Advance Metals and Sky Metals recently proposed combining five Victorian and New South Wales gold projects into a new ASX-listed explorer targeting a $6 million IPO. That proposed transaction highlights the appeal of consolidating exploration assets into separately funded vehicles rather than leaving them embedded within diversified small-cap companies. In addition to the free share distribution, eligible Broken Hill shareholders will get a priority offer to subscribe for up to $2 million of the Manda IPO for around four million shares, if they wish to follow the Queensland promise. Broken Hill’s board has unanimously recommended that its shareholders vote in favour of the capital reduction to allow the in-specie distribution, which will add an extra $32 million in paper valuation upon listing.

Advertisement

Broken Hill Gold managing director Matthew Boyes said: “This is an important value-creation event for Broken Hill Gold shareholders. I encourage shareholders to read the Manda IPO Prospectus in full.” Following the demerger of its Queensland assets, Broken Hill will become exclusively focused on its flagship White Dam project in South Australia’s Curnamona province. Management says the project provides a clear pathway to modest oxide gold production that could help fund the company’s emerging copper-gold district. The company believes it has an early-mover advantage in the region, having secured key tenure with potential for significant discoveries. The project has more than 50 prospects, many lightly tested at depth, with more than 30,000m of RC and diamond drilling planned to probe its deeper gold-copper potential. White Dam historically produced 180,000 ounces between 2010 and 2018 and comes with open pits, heap-leach infrastructure and an operational gold extraction plant, giving the company a brownfields springboard rather than a standing-start development. The near-mine grounds span Vertigo and Hannaford alongside the emerging Icebreaker gold-copper discovery, with existing processing infrastructure providing a ready pathway for shallow oxide material.

Advertisement

The Manda spin-out looks like a classic value-unlocking play, leaving Broken Hill Gold shareholders with exposure to the flagship Icebreaker gold-copper discovery while handing them a free-carried stake in a newly funded Queensland gold explorer. With Manda expected to hit the ASX boards in early January, investors will soon get to put a price on both sides of the split – and decide whether the whole is worth more than the sum of its parts. Ben Carroll’s hopes of leaning on Labor’s economic legacy to hold on to power at the state election have been dealt a blow by figures showing Victoria is the nation’s economic laggard. Figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics released on Wednesday showed the state’s economy grew by 1.7 per cent through 2025-26. Premier Ben Carroll speaking with voters at a pre-poll centre in his electorate. Louis Trerise Every other state and territory posted stronger growth, led by the Northern Territory, which expanded by 3.2 per cent, and Queensland at 3.1 per cent. The nation’s largest state economy, NSW, grew by 2.1 per cent. On a per-capita basis, Victoria was also dragging down the national economic chain with zero growth. The best performers were the NT and Tasmania, which grew by 1.6 per cent. In NSW, it was 0.9 per cent.

Advertisement

Separate data released on Wednesday showed wages grew by 3.3 per cent in Victoria in the 12 months to September. Only the ACT registered slower wage growth. After inflation, Victorian wages fell by 0.2 per cent through the year. Carroll, who attended the pre-polling booth this morning, struggled to talk around a previous Labor voter upset at the business conditions facing him and the state. “Well, I had the opportunity to talk to him,” Carroll told reporters about the interaction. “He has been a previous Labor voter, and I wanted to make it very clear he was fairly supportive of me in the new direction.

Advertisement

“That was why I said I am going to cut land tax, I am a pro-business premier, and they’re the conversations that we get to have every day with voters just like him.” But pressed on whether he had changed the voter’s mind, Carroll admitted failure. “[I] don’t think I convinced him at the end,” he said. “He was very respectful, and it was a good conversation. He knew who I was, knew my background, but that’s democracy.” Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said the state economy was struggling because of the government’s tax policies.

Advertisement

“After 12 years of Labor, Victoria has the weakest economic growth of any state or territory and the weakest wage growth of any state in the country,” she said. “Our population is growing, but economic output per Victorian is going nowhere.” Victoria’s performance last financial year was held back by a sharp fall in mining activity amid a drop in oil and gas production. The strongest part of the economy was financial and insurance services, while there was also a lift in healthcare and social assistance demand. An increase in school and university construction also bolstered the economy. The 1.7 per cent rise last year followed growth of 1.6 per cent in 2024-25 and 1.5 per cent the previous year.

Advertisement

Over the past decade, Victoria’s performance has been one of the strongest in the Commonwealth. Since 2015-16, the economy has grown by almost 27 per cent, eclipsing NSW (21.7 per cent), Western Australia (19.4 per cent), South Australia (25.2 per cent) and the NT (14.8 per cent). The fastest growing part of the country over the past decade has been the ACT, where the economy has expanded by more than 40 per cent. On a per-capita basis, Victoria’s growth of 8.4 per cent has also outperformed jurisdictions including NSW (8.1 per cent), Queensland (7.1 per cent) and the NT (4.8 per cent). The weakest has been Western Australia, where on a per-capita basis, state economic output has fallen by 1.1 per cent. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. I’ve been a racehorse trainer for more than 30 years and never in my life have I seen a deceased horse dumped in a skip bin – until Tuesday. The photos and videos of Melbourne Cup runner So You Are being disposed of at a Lucas Heights dump after dying of colic were shocking and disturbing, and everyone in the racing industry I’ve spoken to in the past 48 hours feels the same way. So You Are, ridden by Rachel King, parades prior to the running of the Lexus Melbourne Cup at Flemington. Racing Photos via Getty Images No animal deserves to be treated that way, and now the spotlight is on industry leaders to see how they respond. We live on a property, and for different reasons, we have had to have horses put down here. We have quite a big property so we bury horses properly when we can, and take comfort in knowing we’re doing the right thing and respecting the horse.

Advertisement

When a horse has to be put down at a veterinary clinic – and that happens quite a lot too – I always thought they would bury them because they charge you, and so you believe they are being disposed of properly. To find out that’s not the case, at least in this instance, is shocking. In all my time in racing, and having grown up around horses, I have never heard of anything like this happening. So You Are was found dumped in a skip bin at Lucas Heights in Sydney. Facebook This kind of incident is also extremely damaging to the racing industry, and it’s not the kind of practice we want to see. We love our horses, and the past 48 hours have been frustrating and sad. There’s got to be a better way. The fact is, disposing of a deceased horse is a problem for any horse owner, not just racehorse owners. But So You Are was a racehorse, and because the racing industry is so big, people will be looking to it.

Advertisement

There is no doubt Racing NSW is on the front foot and looking at what it can do to make sure this doesn’t happen again. The situation here is black and white and something has to change. Knowing what we know now, that it is common practice for horses to end up in landfill, there needs to be reforms to how we dispose of deceased horses. One idea is for the industry to invest in a crematorium, so trainers, owners and jockeys know their racehorses are being treated with dignity in death. That would also mean that deceased horses wouldn’t be taking up space in landfill, and horrific situations like what we’ve seen in the past 48 hours wouldn’t occur.

For most of us in the industry, we are part of racing because we love horses, not just the competition. Related Article Opinion

Racing integrity So You Are’s horrifying final fate in a skip bin with an old couch is beyond unacceptable Neil Breen National sports editor We’ve got about 20 horses in work at the moment, but we are constantly getting horses and retiring horses. Some are become broodmares and some are just nice horses we keep around the farm because we love them. But for the most part, we spend a significant amount of time, money and effort into retraining and re-homing them so they have long lives and good homes. It makes me so happy to see my horses have another life after racing. Reform won’t happen overnight, but from the time a horse is born to the time of its death, everything should be done respectfully, and I think a crematorium would be a good way to make things work.

Working Australians buying homes have endured a year of falling real wages on top of soaring mortgage repayments as signs grow the economy will struggle into 2027. The Australian Bureau of Statistics this morning reported the wage price index rose by a higher-than-expected 1.1 per cent in the September quarter. Real wages have gone backwards for the fourth consecutive quarter. Oscar Colman It was driven by this year’s minimum wage increase of 4.75 per cent and was the largest quarterly increase since the end of 2023. It took annual wage growth to 3.5 per cent. Despite that, inflation through to the September quarter was 3.9 per cent. It meant in real terms, wages went backwards by 0.4 per cent. It was the fourth successive quarterly negative result for real wages.

Advertisement

Apart from the minimum wage increase, a series of state-based pay increases to frontline public servants including nurses, midwives and police officers contributed to the out-sized quarterly result. Related Article Live

National News Live Australia news as it happened: Labor blames high inflation for falling wages; Cook cuts deal to exempt WA gas from national scheme Treasurer Jim Chalmers said nominal wages growth had exceeded 3 per cent for 17 consecutive quarters, the first time they had been that strong for 17 years. “Labor’s support for higher wages is helping almost 2.8 million workers on the national minimum wage, up to 460,000 health, disability and community services workers and the 400,000 strong aged care work force,” he said. Wages for the bottom 20 per cent of earners rose by 4.7 per cent over the past 12 months, largely due to the minimum wage increase, while for the next 20 per cent they grew by 3.9 per cent.

Advertisement

But deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume said once inflation was taken into account, Australians were going backwards. “[The] figures confirm what every Australian already knows: their pay packet buys less now than it did when Labor came to office. Australians aren’t just feeling poorer, they are poorer,” she said. Since mid-2022, soon after the government took office, inflation has climbed by a combined 18.2 per cent. Over that same period, wages have increased by 16.2 per cent. That followed the Morrison government period in office when real wages also went backwards. Over the past 8 years, wages have grown by 25.9 per cent compared to inflation which has risen by 31.5 per cent.

Advertisement

The figures were released as Westpac’s measure of economic activity in coming months fell into negative territory. The bank is now expecting economic growth to slow to 1.4 per cent in 2026 and the drop to just one per cent next year. EY chief economist Cherelle Murphy said while the wage figures would not prompt an immediate response from the Reserve Bank. “The figure is uncomfortably high for the central bank but is unlikely to prompt any immediate reaction given the economy is now slowing in response to the five interest rate hikes delivered between February and November this year,” she said. “The Reserve Bank is tackling the challenge by aggressively trying to bring inflation down. Given the significant rise in the cash rate from 3.6 to 4.85 per cent this year, we expect the central bank will be in wait-and-see mode.” That could be challenged by job figures due out on Thursday. Unemployment has lifted to a five-year high of 4.7 per cent, with forward indicators suggesting the jobs market is slowing.

Advertisement

The single largest increase was for people in the hospitality sector, which is broadly covered by the minimum wage decision. Wages for these workers lifted by 3.4 per cent in the quarter to be 4.1 per cent up over the year. Wages in the education sector are the slowest growing in the country, up 0.8 per cent in the quarter but just 2.6 per cent over the past 12 months. Professional services (2.7 per cent) and those in administration and financial services (both 2.9 per cent) are also a long way behind inflation. Private sector wages rose to 3.4 per cent while public sector wages lifted by 3.9 per cent over the past year. title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
